CANADIAN ARMY-PERSONNEL ENLISTED FOR OVERSEAS BUT STILL IN CANADA
speechtext:
1.	How many men who enlisted in the army for overseas service are there at present in Canada?
2.	Of these, how many are, (a) members of the veterans guard; (b) in categories which render them unsuitable for overseas service; (c) are necessarily retained in this country for organizational or staff duties?
Mr. MACDONALD (Halifax);
1.	Including those in territories adjacent to Canada, approximately 140,000 of whom probably 50,000 or more are or can be made available as reinforcements for overseas service.
2.	(a) Approximately 8,500.
(b)	Excluding those in the veterans guard there are approximately 50,000 who are of an age or military category such that they would not normally be sent overseas. Individuals among these may be sent overseas for special duty.
In addition, there are approximately 25,000 who, while not definitely unsuitable for overseas service, are in age groups, medical categories, or ranks such that only a limited number of them can be absorbed within establishments of the army overseas.
(c)	Excluding those referred to in (a) and (b) above, there are approximately 10,000 employed on the staffs of administrative, training and servicing units in Canada.
As many as possible of these are being withdrawn for overseas service, but some will no doubt have to be retained permanently in Canada because their duties require fit general service volunteers or because of special knowledge and experience which makes it difficult to obtain suitable replacements.

1.	If a soldier purchases a victory bond on the instalment plan and is posted as missing, what happens in regard to the unpaid balance?
2.	If a soldier purchasing victory bonds on the instalment plan is killed before completing the transaction, what happens to the amount paid on the bond?
3.	Is it refunded to the next of kin?
4.	If so, is the interest allowed?

Mr. MACDONALD (Halifax);
1 and 2. When a soldier is missing or dies.
(a)	If the casualty occurred prior to the end of the fifth month of the instalment period and advice thereof is received prior to the end of the sixth (and final) month of the instalment period, the assignment of pay for the purchase of the bond is cancelled retroactive to its commencement and the instalments so far deducted are recredited to the soldier's pay account. Where such advice is not received prior to the end of the sixth (and final) month, purchase of the bond would be cpmpleted.
(b)	If the casualty occurred during the sixth (and final) month of the instalment period purchase of the bond would be completed.
(Note: Under article 83 F.R. & I. (Canada) the pay and allowances (except subsistence allowance) of a soldier who dies or is reported missing are credited to the end of the month in which the casualty occurs. Therefore, the purchase of a bond is completed only in those cases where the casualty occurred during the sixth month or where advice of a casualty which occurred prior thereto is received subsequent to the end of the sixth month. In the latter case, an overpayment of assigned pay results which may be recovered from any credit balance accruing in the soldier's pay account.)
3.	In those cases where the death, etc. of the soldier necessitates cancellation of the assignment of pay, the deductions recredited to the pay account form part of the service estate of the soldier and are transferred to the administrator of estates for distribution to those entitled thereto by law. This procedure is in accordance with the terms of the soldier's application for purchase of the bond.
Where purchase of the bond has been completed the person entitled thereto will receive the bond in accordance with the instructions given by the soldier in his application for purchase of the bond, or if the bond is deposited with the Department of Finance for safekeeping, that department will surrender it to the administrator of estates for inclusion in the service estate of the soldier.
4.	Where purchase of a bond is completed, the interest accrues to those entitled thereto, either by receipt of the bond itself, or through distribution of the soldier's service estate.
In those cases where the purchase of a bond by assignment of pay is cancelled owing to the death, etc., of the soldier, pro rata payments of interest on the instalments recredited to the pay account are not made as no authority exists for such payments, nor are they provided for in the terms of the soldier's application for purchase of a bond.

radio BROADCASTING-COMPLIMENTARY DINNER TO THE PRIME MINISTER ON AUGUST 7

In view of the fact that, on the evening of the 7th of August next, there will he a political rally at the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa, and a provincial election will be held in Quebec on the 8th of August, what means will the government take to prevent, on those two occasions, infringement of section 22, subsection 4 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act of 1936?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
perhaps I had better answer this question. It evidently relates to the recognition of the twenty-fifth anniversary of my appointment as leader of the Liberal party by my fellow members in parliament who are generously tendering me a complimentary dinner on that evening at the Chateau Laurier.
It is not a surprise, then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to
my hon. friend that it was a surprise to me to see references in the papers to matters pertaining to this occasion of which I had no knowledge whatever. Among others was a reference to the fact that a nation-wide broadcast would be made by myself on that evening.

National
headquarters got the wires crossed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No-if my
hon. friend will just be courteous and allow me to make my statement. I should like to have the position made perfectly clear. When I sawT in the press the statement that at the dinner there would be a broadcast by myself I immediately felt that some persons, perhaps a good many more than I had reason to feel might so regard it, might think that the occasion had been arranged from some political motive and that any address or remarks by myself on that evening would be made for purposes of furthering some political end.
I immediately ascertained who among my friends had the matter more immediately in hand. I not only spoke to them, but I put myself on record in a letter in which I stated that much as I appreciated the compliment of the dinner I felt I would have to decline to make any broadcast on that occasion, that were I to do so my own motives and the motives of the party would most certainly be mistaken. I asked that as some announcement had been made in the press to the effect that I would be broadcasting on that evening, a correction be made. I gave as my reasons not merely the possible misconstruction that might be placed on a broadcast at that time, but also my feeling that with the war at the stage at which it is at the present, I was the last one who would wish to be responsible in
any way for possible further political controversy at this time. Moreover I pointed out that there was likely to be a provincial election; in fact, a provincial election in the province of Quebec had been mentioned. It was some days ago that I spoke of this matter. Since then it has been decided to hold provincial elections in both Alberta and New Brunswick. It is natural that some persons should have minds akin to that of the hon. member who has asked this question. I pointed out such persons would assume of course that there must be something sinister and ulterior about the proposed recognition of the occasion in the manner suggested.
I have noticed in this morning's paper the following statement which I think puts the matter in its true light. I shall quote it as I believe it has been sent to the press generally throughout Canada:
A speech Prime Minister Mackenzie King is scheduled to deliver August 7 at a dinner marking the 25th anniversary of his leadership of the Liberal party will not be broadcast, it was announced last night.
The committee in charge of arrangements for the dinner said in a statement that an earlier announcement that the speech would be broadcast over the national network of the C.B.C. was made before consultation with the Prime Minister.
The statement added that Mr. King felt that any broadcast which might be made "would almost certainly be construed as having a political motive and as such might give rise to political controversy." This, Mr. King is most anxious to avoid . . . particularly at this stage of the war and at a time when elections are being held in three of the provinces of Canada.
(Elections will be held in Quebec and Alberta August 8 and in New Brunswick August 28.)
I hope that what I have said and what appears in the press will be sufficient to make perfectly clear that neither the committee in charge of this complimentary dinner nor I myself have any desire to make political capital out of this recognition by my fellow members in parliament of the 25th anniversary of my election as leader of the Liberal party of Canada.

Perhaps I may be given the opportunity to add a word which the Prime Minister himself could not say because he did not know anything about it. The arrangements for the complimentary dinner for the Prime Minister were taken in hand over eight months ago. The Prime Minister knew nothing whatever about it, but from the beginning it was contemplated that it would be a proper occasion on which he might make a speech to the country over the radio. These assumptions and inferences, that this is something that has been arranged to influence the present political situation, are wholly without foundation whatever.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTIONS-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to bill No. 135, to provide regulations enabling Canadian war service electors to exercise their franchise, and Canadian prisoners of war to vote by proxy, at any general election held during the present war, also to provide amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, consequential to such regulations, or made necessary by the advent of the said war.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the other house has returned this bill with two amendments. I shall not at this stage deal with them at any length but might explain them briefly.
The first amendment is to section 5, by adding the words, "at the time of the passing of this act". The intention and effect of that is that in the event of any provincial legislature deciding that it should disqualify electors by reason of racial origin between the time of the passing of this act and the next election, this amendment will not prevent the affected parties mentioned in such measure from voting.
The next amendment is to section 11. That section deals with those clauses of the bill that will apply only to an election held within the present war and within a period of six months thereafter. I think from the wording of section 5 it might be argued, in fact it is made clear that it could apply only at the time this country is at war, because it states specifically that any disqualifications are those of a country which is at war with Canada. Members of this house, especially legal members, will agree that a statute always speaks in the present tense, but notwithstanding that, the endeavour has been made to make it clearer. I believe, Mr. Speaker, there is no objection to concurrence in the amendment. It might be argued that it makes assurance doubly sure and there could be no exception taken to that. Consequently I am prepared to move concurrence in the amendment. But
I also wish to move another amendment consequential to the senate amendment, and that is:
That the following words be added to the words "at the time of the passing of this act": "namely, July 1, 1938, and on the date of the declaration of such war resided in a province in which on those dates."
The effect of that is simply this. There has been some criticism of the disqualification of certain members of the Japanese race even though we are in the midst of a bitter and grim war, and the result of this amendment will be that no one who has enjoyed the right to vote will be disqualified. In other words, the right of the Japanese race to vote will be unimpaired in so far as they previously enjoyed that right. I believe this will meet the situation. I do not think, no matter how broadminded we may be, that at a time of war we should consider extending the franchise to those of an enemy race, and any other provision in the act will unquestionably have that effect. This leaves the right of those of the Japanese race who had the right to vote unimpaired, untrammelled, and uninterfered with. I believe that will meet with general approval in all sections of the house, and I consequently move that the senate amendment be concurred in as well as the motion I have proposed.

brief statement that the committee on war service voters regulations were unanimous in their approval, which was quite correct. Most of the members who served on the committee drafting war service voters regulations had no knowledge of the matter now before the house.

That is right. Therefore, when the Secretary of State introduced the resolution in the house on June 8 there was no bill. Second reading was given to the bill on June 9. There was still no bill in the hands of the members of this house when it was given second reading. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked whether it had been printed or not. The reason I mention this is that every member of this house is desirous of correcting a mistake that was made at that time. At the time I spoke on the bill I had not seen it. I came to the house at a moment's notice. The matter was under discussion. I thought the bill merely had to do with the matters that the committee on war service voters regulations had passed on; and without any reservation I gave my support to the bill. After getting a chance to sit down and go over the bill I was surprised to see that this addition had been made. What I am concerned with is something that should not have been done in this bill, namely, to include amendments to the elections act which greatly change the exercise of the franchise in a federal election.
I think it was the wrong place to make the amendment. It should not be pinned to the war service voters regulations. As one member of the committee who studied that question, I merely wish to make it clear that had we had knowledge of that proposal and if there had been an opportunity to discuss it it certainly would not have received my support in any way, shape or form.
The amendment made by the senate does not, in my opinion, cover the objection, and the amendment now made by the Secretary of State does not clarify it to my satisfaction. What I am concerned about is that in the exercise of the franchise in Canada we are still practising racial discrimination, a? the bill now stands. While we know that the war with Japan is a serious matter and that many atrocities have been committed by the people of that country, there is no reason why we should try to duplicate the performances of that country. Canada is a country that is made up largely of minority groups. From day to day we read of the atrocities committed by Germany against our prisoners, people who are helpless to defend themselves. No one

has ever suggested that we should interfere with the exercise of the franchise by German residents of this country.

Every person residing in Canada whose racial origin is that of a country at war with Canada, if such person, at the time of the passing of this act: namely, July 1, 1938, and on the date of the declaration of such war, resided in a province in which on those dates a person of his racial origin was disqualified from voting at an election of a member of the legislative assembly of that province, and who did not serve in the naval, military or air forces of Canada in the war of 1914-1918, or in any subsequent war in which Canada may be engaged.

speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt; I will not do it again. You cannot take away from a person something he did not have. To keep the record straight the date is July 1, 1938, which is the date of the passing of the general elections act; but the effective date is the date of the declaration of war with the Japanese empire.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTIONS-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: May we understand clearly what my hon. friend is asking? Is he asking that Japanese who had no right to vote in a federal election prior to the war shall now be given the right to vote if they happen to be in some part of Canada other than British Columbia? That is the point. Does he want that? If that is what he wishes, let him state it. Let him explain what he means. Is he asking for the conferring of the right to vote on a large number of Japanese who would not have that right had they not been moved for reasons connected with the war and for the security of Canada during the war?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTIONS-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is exactly what I am
asking, Mr. Speaker, and I am going to state my opinions on the matter, very briefly. I believe that any person who was permitted to enter this country and become a citizen of it should have the full rights of citizenship. That is my opinion, and that is particularly so in regard to those born in Canada, who are Canadians because of that fact.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTIONS-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit a question, is that the hon. member's personal opinion, or is it the official opinion of the party?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTIONS-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is official, from the
party.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTIONS-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Does that apply to
British Columbia, too?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTIONS-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I hope you will note these
interruptions, Mr. Speaker. I am not speaking for British Columbia; I am speaking for the members of this group.
Dominion Elections
, If the hon. member does not so wish, he may not be interrupted.
Thank you. I am not concerned about the Japanese only; I am concerned about the people of every racial origin in this country.	,
The Japanese are the only ones involved.

Yes; you are practising racial discrimination so far as this particular group is concerned. There is something else I want to make clear. I remember vividly the fight that was put up thirty-five or forty years ago when the Japanese were brought into this country; certain sections of Canada did their best to keep them out. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company and other employers in this country were concerned with bringing them in so that they might obtain cheap labour to serve their purposes.
Not the Japanese; the Chinese.

That has been denied
time and again.

It would not be very hard
to dig back into the records and prove that statement. The present attitude is a surprise to me in view of what I find in Hansard, in booklets and pamphlets issued by the Liberal party, and in official statements by the Conservative party. These statements are very liberal, and I think they indicate the policy that must be followed if we are to make progress in the future. This country has to be populated. We have no Japanese in Nova Scotia-

No; that is the
reason.

If we think we, eleven and a half million people on this half of the continent of North America, can set ourselves up as a super race and bring in slaves to work for us, at the same time denying them the rights of citizenship, certainly that is not in accordance with statements made in this house by both the Liberal and Conservative parties. I am much concerned, Mr. Speaker, when those who are conducting the affairs of this nation can make a statement this year and twist it around next year, particularly when it has to do with basic principles, without any regard to what was said the year before. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is a British Columbia member. I should like to quote the opinion he expressed on a former occasion. I refer to page 4487 of Hansard for June 29, 1934, when

the Dominion Franchise Act was under discussion in relation to the Doukhobors. The minister had this to say:
If these people refuse to obey our laws they should be punished, but I think disfranchisement is the wrong form of punishment. It is. an invidious distinction. I hold no brief for these people as I think they deserved the *punishment which the attorney general and the government of the day in British Columbia meted out to them, but I think it is a bad precedent for this parliament to follow'.
The minister was very anxious at that time to protect the right of the franchise with respect to a minority group. Again, at page 4530 of Hansard for June 30, 1934, I find this discussion:
Mr. Bennett: ... If they are not willing to become citizens of Canada and openly defy the lawr, then they should not be permitted to vote as citizens.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	In view of what the
Prime Minister has just said, may I ask him this question:	Would not a better way to
proceed have been to enact in the franchise act that any person who defies the law' to the extent of refusing to be enumerated as a Canadian citizen shall not be qualified to vote?
Mr. Bennett:	That cannot be done.
The portion of the discussion with which I am. concerned follows:
Mr. Mackenzie King: Then innocent parties should not be discriminated against, or as Burke says, you cannot indict a nation; no more can you indict an entire race or all members of any religious sect.
I agree with that statement. In the last thirty years I have had some considerable experience with many minority groups in Canada, and I think I am safe in saying that most of such groups, and this includes the Japanese, came to this country as refugees from the order of society which has developed in those countries. Hon. members may say that is not so. Discuss the matter with them individually and personally. They are prepared to obey the laws of Canada. Many of them have taken out citizenship papers. Thousands were born in this country. To-day many of them: are fighting in the army of the United States. They are not in the Canadian army because they are not permitted to join it. During the last war I served with a unit which had as reinforcements part of a battalion of Japanese raised in British Columbia, and we considered them to be very competent soldiers. At least five Purple Hearts have 'been won by Japanese soldiers with the American armies fighting the legions of Mussolini in Italy.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, there was never a battalion of Japanese raised in British Columbia.

Dominion Elections
Only seventy-four Japanese enlisted in all Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; over two hundred.
I am not going to argue with hon. members, but I remember distinctly getting reinforcements in October, 1916, which consisted of about 175 Japanese from British Columbia.	'
Japan was our ally then.

That is all right. Thousands of Japanese who are in Canada to-day came here at or about that, time, and they have been living here ever since, making their contribution. As I said before, when you start to interfere with the liberties of one section of the people of Canada the time is coming when it will apply to every section. It is really a matter of setting a precedent. My stand -is that if we permit a man to enter this country, give him the right to work and accept him as a citizen, we are under an obligation to go all the way with him. If we keep these people segregated in their own groups, refuse them the right of citizenship and so on, how can we expect to make citizens of them? If we are not going to make citizens of them certainly we should not have them in the country. Either they should be here on the basis of full citizenship or they should not be here at all.
I have no doubt it was in the rush of business that this thing got through the house. I should like to see section 5 deleted completely, but I know that cannot be done at this point. The only thing we can do is attempt to correct the senate amendment in the best way possible to meet the situation. In that connection I am going to move a subamendment, seconded by Mr. Knowles:
That all the words of the amendment moved by the Secretary of State after the word "that" be deleted, and the following substituted therefor:
"the motion for concurrence in the senate amendment to clause 5 be amended as follows: That the word 'the' after the word 'at' in the proposed amendment be struck out and the word 'a' Substituted therefor, -and that all the words after the word 'time' be struck out and the following words substituted therefore: 'subsequent to the next general election'."
I have no intention of going into a long debate in the matter. I merely wish to make it clear that, we are opposed to racial discrimination in any way, shape or form as applied to any section of Canada where minority groups are accepted as citizens. This subamendment merely means that section 5 of the present bill would remain inoperative in the next general election. The matter would remain as
it is, or as it was prior to the passing of this Section of the bill. By the time this house convenes again there may be a new parliament. But if it is not a new parliament, the members of the house have the right and privilege of going into the elections act and tightening the act as they may wish, or changing it completely. What I wish to make clear is that we are not satisfied with it, and we want to try to undo any harm that was done in the rush of putting this bill through the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On a point of order, from what my hon. friend has said at the very conclusion of his remarks it would seem that his amendment is intended to leave matters as they were prior to the carrying of section 5. That, as I understand it, is the intention of my hon. friend's amendment. If that is so, its effect is the same thing as that of the amendment moved by the Secretary of State. Therefore, being to all intents and purposes the same amendment in its effect, it could not be considered by the house.
In what I am saying I have referred to what I understood the hon. member to have said about his amendment. I am not referring to anything he may have had to say with regard to the general question of the right of all persons to vote. That is another matter.

I shall read the subamendment-. It is as follows:
That all the words of the amendment moved by the Secretary of State after the word "that" be deleted, and the following substituted therefor:
"the motion for concurrence in the senate amendment to clause 5 be amended as follows: That the word 'the' after the word 'at' in the proposed amendment be struck out and the word 'a' substituted therefor, and that all the words after the word 'time' be struck out and the following words substituted therefor:	'subsequent to the next general election'."
This would mean that the following words be added: "At a time subsequent to the next general election". That is the effect of the subamendment.
Mr. Speaker, would you read section 5 as amended?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, let us have that.

Section 5, as proposed, would be as follows:
Every person residing in Canada whose racial origin is that of a country at war with Canada, if such person, -at the time of the passing of this act, namely July I, 1938, and on the date of the declaration of such war, resided in a province in which on those dates a person of his racial origin was disqualified from voting at an election of a member of the legislative assembly of
Dominion Elections

that province, and who did not serve in the naval, military or air forces of Canada in the war of 1914-18 or in any subsequent war in which Canada may be engaged.

That extends the
franchise.
Mr. Speaker, would you read the amendment again?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, let us have it again.

The amendment by the hon. member for Cape Breton South is:
That all the words of the amendment moved by the Secretary of State after the word "that" be deleted-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: From what?-from the amendment?

I would suppose that would mean from the section of the bill. It states:
That all the words of the amendment moved by the Secretary of State after the word "that" be deleted, and the following substituted therefor:
"The motion for concurrence in the senate amendment to clause 5 be amended as follows: That the word 'the' after the word 'at' in the proposed amendment be struck out and the word 'a' substituted therefor, and that all the words after the word 'time' be struck out and the following words substituted therefor: 'subsequent to the next general election'."

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The intention of that amendment is therefore obvious. The disqualification does not refer to a disqualification previously existing from July 1, 1938, or at the outbreak of war. The disqualification would refer to a time after the holding of the next election.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is destructive, completely, of the principle now before the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am glad to have that admission. This is a direct negative, and therefore I submit it is not in order.

I am not inclined to agree that the hon. member intends a direct negative. I take it that it would read so that all the words of the amendment moved by the Secretary of State would be deleted, and it would substitute therefor "at a time subsequent to the next general election."

Mr. Speaker, I rise to another point of order, if you have decided the first one. I would refer to citation 589 in Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms,
CMr. Speaker.]
second edition. We are now dealing with an amendment to a vote for concurrence, which is rather an unusual thing. It is laid down in this citation that-
No amendment can be proposed to the senate's amendment save an amendment strictly relevant thereto; nor can an amendment be moved to the bill, unless the amendment foe relevant to or consequent upon either the acceptance or the rejection of a senate amendment.
I suggest that this proposed amendment is not relevant to the amendments, nor is it consequent upon them. The word "consequent" means following upon. Taken literally, "consequent" would mean that if a motion were proposed to strike out section 4, and in the event of that section being stricken out it became necessary to renumber the following sections,. an amendment to renumber would be " consequent." It would be a trivial correction consequent upon having accepted another amendment. We might then have to renumber certain sections. The proposal of the hon. member for Cape Breton South is not consequent, nor is it particularly relevant. It might be relevant, but it certainly is not consequent. Then, let us look at the bill. Hon. members know that explanations are written on the right hand pages in the bill. That is the law. The explanation appearing opposite this section reads:
This provides a disqualification from voting at a dominion election of persons of the Japanese race.
Those are the words which explain what section 5 means. The speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South indicates that he wishes that the Japanese shall vote. Therefore it cannot in any sense be held to be consequent. I suggest therefore that it is not consequent, that it is not relevant, and that it is out of order.

The amendment which I have read already, and the amendment to the amendment, would read as follows:
Every .person residing in Canada whose racial origin is that of a country at war with Canada at .a time subsequent to the next general election-
That is the amendment. Then the amendment moved by the hon. member deletes all the words following and its result would be that the section would then convey no meaning. It would not mean that any person of that racial origin would have the right to vote, because it deletes the following words:

and on the date of the declaration of such war, resided in a province in which on those dates a person of his racial origin was disqualified from voting at an election of a member of the legislative assembly of that province,

Dominion Elections
and who did not serve in the naval, military or air forces of Canada in the war of 1914-18 or in any subsequent war in which Canada was engaged.
Those words are struck out and therefore the amendment as proposed conveys nothing. It makes no provision for voting, and therefore it is not in order.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Do I understand, Mr. Speaker,
that you have ruled the amendment out of order?
Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Speaking then to the
motion of the Secretary of State for the adoption of the senate amendment as amended by the Secretary of State, I should like to make a few comments. It seems to me that what is at stake here to-day is not so much the rights of certain Japanese Canadians who have moved from British Columbia to other parts of Canada, as the basic concept of democracy and our integrity as a nation so far as our belief in the franchise is concerned I feel I should take a moment or two to place on the record some quotations relevant to this question of disfranchising a group of people by race.
I hold in my hand a bound volume of political pamphlets which I obtained from the library and which includes a musty document entitled, "The Liberal Point of View. Current Comment on the Proceedings of the Parliamentary Session of 1920." I should like to read from that document, as follows:
The great principle underlying the present franchise law is that all men and women shall vote-that the basis of the franchise shall be humanity. Still there are members and members of parliament who cling to the notion that they are dispensing a sort of charity when they allow- men and women to vote-that they are political almsgivers-that they have the right to pick and choose and say who is to vote and who is not to vote.
I will skip a sentence or two which had to do with the political situation existing at the time, then I quote further:
The franchise law

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend had better read the part he is omitting, so that we shall have the full text

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Perhaps the Prime Minister is right. The part I intended to omit reads:
The pretension is all the more ridiculous when it is remembered that the present government and the members of parliament upon whose support it relies are mere usurpers, who in a fair and democratic election would be shorn of their power by the voice of the people.
I was sparing the right hon. gentleman that sentence. I continue:
The franchise law contains a lot of pedantic rubbish about "aliens", which the Liberals-
My whole point in speaking to-day is that many liberals-I use the small "1"-are with us on this. I continue:

and other progressive members of the house haw tried to clear away. The House of Commons, not as a despotic ruler, but as a trustee for the people, may have a right to associate good citizenship with the franchise. Good citizenship is not a matter of race or birth. It is a matter of conduct. It is a matter of the relationship of a man towards his family and his neighbours and the community in which he lives. Any one of the constituencies which elect representatives to parliament is probably a better judge of these qualifications than parliament itself. The duty of fixing the qualifications is assigned to parliament in a general way. But parliament is only a referee and should do its duty modestly, not in an arrogant fashion.
The man of foreign or alien birth or descent is in a peculidr position. He came to us with traditions that are European rather than Canadian. He came upon our invitation. We ought not to have invited him unless we expected to make him a good citizen of Canada, for we do not want men and women in Canada who, as Mr. Pardee says, are in no man's land.
There is a great deal of talk of Canadianizing the foreigner and make him a good citizen. All right if we are sincere, and if we carry our ideas to their logical conclusion. If we desire to educate the foreigner or the alien, we must assume toward him an attitude of sympathy and confidence, not of suspicion. We should invite him to our councils. We should tell him that the institutions of our country, our legislative bodies and courts are his institutions too, that they are intended to protect him and promote his interests and that we want him to take his part in framing and maintaining them.
It is an extremely foolish notion that by depriving a man of alien birth or descent, of the vote, we can keep him out of mischief. If there were a really vicious malignant enemy of Canada in our midst, he would not care whether he had a vote or not. He would take no pride in citizenship. He would not desire to have a part in working the institutions of the countries. He would prefer to see those institutions destroyed. The man or woman who is really hurt by defranchisement is the man or woman who is friendly to Canada, who wants to be a citizen, who desires to have a part in working the institutions of Canada. Deprive such a man or woman of the franchise and you may convert a friend into an enemy, or at least quench the flame of friendship and patriotism and create a class of man and woman who will be indifferent to Canadianism. Let us take the opposite course. Let us kindle the flames of Canadianism and patriotism by a policy of friendship and confidence toward men of every race and creed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend made some reference to myself. Was he intimating that I had written that particular document?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not believe that I associated the Prime Minister's name particularly with the authorship of this document.

Dominion Elections

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend said that he was sparing my feelings for some reason. It is a very good document.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was referring to the sentence I had left out, to the effect that the government had not the confidence of the people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the document my hon. friend is reading from?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Here is its full title:
The Liberal Point of View.
Current Comment on the Proceedings of the Parliamentary Session of 1920.
National Liberal Committee, 115 Sparks Street, Ottawa.
Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, M.P., Liberal Leader.
Andrew Haydon, National Organizer and General Secretary.
John Lewis, Editor of Liberal Publications.
Publication No. 4-Issued June 15.
I suggest that my right hon. friend look it over himself, because there is a lot of good stuff in it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is a document written by the late Senator John Lewis, and I think it is an excellent document.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I would remind the Prime Minister that in 1917, when somewhat similar circumstances prevailed before the house, his former leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, moved the following motion on September 10 of that year:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that the abridgement by this parliament of the electoral franchise now enjoyed in any province of the dominion by any class of His Majesty's subjects would be contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
Had we caught this clause on the second reading of the bill nothing would have been more proper at that time than to move the amendment moved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1917 and in exactly those words. Unfortunately with the way things happened on June 9 it is now necessary for parliament to try to fix this up in the best way possible. My hon. friends who know me sometimes criticize me because I watch things in too great detail. I confess that I do it, but I missed that one completely. Why? Because we were given assurances inside and outside of the house that what we had before us in bill No. 135 was the enactment of the work that had been done by the special committee on which my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) sat.

I must correct the hon. member in that. In my remarks before the committee of the whole I made it perfectly

clear that the part which the committee had dealt with, and the only part, was schedule 1 of the bill; that the committee had made a recommendation in regard to schedule 2 but had not considered it clause by clause, and no reference of it to the committee had been made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is exactly the
trouble. No reference was made to it. What happened was this. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) on June 8 asked this question-

It is a misconstruction to say that no reference was made. It was made quite clear that no reference was made to the committee of the wording of the bill itself. I do not mean that no reference was made to the bill, but no reference was made to the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
At no time was any suggestion made that there was such a clause in this bill. I doubt if any private member of the house knew that that clause was in there. We took these assurances because we were not of a suspicious frame of mind. We should have been. People outside the house who now read Hansard and see what happened think that we were asleep. They read Hansard and see that this bill was brought down with this clause in it and that we passed it without saying a word about it.
I go back to the resolution which was introduced by the Secretary of State preceding the introduction of the bill relating to the war service voters, and it reads-now I quote- "to provide amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, consequential to such regulations." Consequently when the bill came before us from the committee, we did not read it in detail because we thought that the only things to be found in it were things consequential to the regulations to provide for the taking of the soldiers' vote. But subsequently the Toronto Saturday Niyht, the Winnipeg Free Press and other papers began to look through the bill and drew this clause to our attention and to the attention of other members of the house and the country generally.
I was going on to point out when I was interrupted that the hon. member for Vancouver South on June 8 asked this question in the house at page 3643 of Hansard:
Will the minister tell us wh ther or not the recommendations have been accepted in full and, if not in full, in what way they have been varied?
Mr. McLarty: I wonder if th" hon. member is referring to the specific regulations adopted by the special committee dealing with war service electors. If he is, they have been

Dominion Elections
adopted in full, as have the provisions which were recommended by the special committee in connection with granting votes by proxy to prisoners of war and those interned in neutral countries. I wonder if that answers the hon. gentleman.
Mr. Green: Apparently the regulations have been adopted in full?
Mr. McLarty: That is correct.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, it is correct, but look how we were put off the track by it. Then the hon. member for Vancouver South went on to ask this question:
Mr. Green: Without any variation?
Mr. McLarty: There might be the change of a word, but nothing material.
When the Secretary of State stated that there was nothing but the change of a word, nothing material, so far as the regulations are concerned, we thought that that covered the whole story. But instead of that here we have this bill with this clause in it which I submit is a violation of the basic traditions of Liberalism down across the years.

On a point of order, there were further questions which I asked of the Secretary of State, and if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will read them he will see that they put a different construction upon the matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am willing to take the time to read them, but you will find nothing there that makes reference to any clause in the bill having anything to do with other than amendments to the soldier vote regulations and consequential amendments. Then we find that there is something that was not consequential at all, and that makes me suggest that the resolution itself was not properly worded in the first instance.

Had not the members of the
house the bill before them at the time of the second reading?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was just coming to
that. On April 26 the report of the committee was tabled. We in our group had studied that report. We held two or three special caucuses upon it, and so we knew just what was in that report. We were satisfied with it. Now to come back to the question which the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) asked, the resolution was passed and the bill introduced and given its first reading on June 8. On that occasion the leader of the opposition asked the Secretary of State if the bill had been printed, and the Secretary of State replied in the affirmative. The next morning several of us tried to get copies of the bill but were unable to do so. Later that day, in
100-309J
the afternoon at three o'clock, the leader of the opposition. rose on the orders of the day and called the attention of the Secretary of State to the fact that he had been told that the bill had been printed but that the members of his group were not able to get a copy of it. The Secretary of State replied that he thought he was stating the facts as he knew them when he made his reply the day before, but that he had found out since that although the bill had been printed it was not yet bound or made available to hon. members. So that we still did not have the bill on June 9. The bill was placed on our desks at the actual moment that second reading was called on the night of June 9. I was here and I have a vivid recollection of it. I had not read the bill and I doubt if any members of the house had read it. We had for six weeks studied the details of the soldiers' vote regulations, which we were assured was all that
the bill dealt with, 'and so long as we.were
satisfied with the regulations we felt that we were doing our full duty.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but he will find at page 3643 of Hansard that it was made amply clear that the committee had dealt only with schedule A, and not with schedule B, and there was no suggestion that the bill was at any time before the special committee. I therefore feel that my hon. friend's suggestion that in some way the thing was hidden from the house is not an honest one or a fair one, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have not said that the bill was before the committee. I have said that it was not before anybody.
The bill was in the hands of the hon. member both at the time of the second reading and in committee of the whole. It was right there in the form in which it is at present.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have often had occasion to object in the house when bills were called for second reading and we did not have a copy of the bill in advance, but I felt that I was making a nuisance of myself always to ask to have these bills before us.

There was no suggestion of urgency on the part of the sponsor of the bill. It was not suggested that there was any hurry or any urgency to get the bill through. It was there just the same as any other bill.

The hon. member for Comox-Alibemi (Mr. Neill) had the bill before him, because he said it contained one and one-half pages and then the schedules. That was on the second reading of the bill.
Dominion Elections
Had the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre read: the explanatory note on section 5 of the bill?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We only got the bill when the second reading was called. We did1 not have it the morning before, as we should have, and we were not suspicious. We did not have any reason to go into the details of the bill because we had gone into the details of the lengthy schedules attached to it.

Explanatory note to section 5, consisting of two lines, was perfectly clear. It reads:
This provides a disqualification from voting at a dominion election of persons of the Japanese race.
There was no suggestion of trying to influence the house improperly. The explanatory note was there and it would not take more than a few seconds to read.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am satisfied that I am not the only member of the house who did not see it in the rush and feels this way about it. There are a good many members with good liberal blood in their veins who, if they had noticed this clause, would have had something to say about it on this occasion. As soon a9 the bill had been given its third reading it was given publicity and there has been a good deal said about it throughout the country. I have already referred to some of the publications, such as Toronto Saturday Night and the Winnipeg Free Press, which have done particularly good work on it. The Free Press has dug up not only the quotations I have referred to but others back in Hansard across the years. The Free Press has this interesting statement to make:
It is certainly to be hoped that British Columbians who call themselves Liberals will not sink to this apostasy of Liberal principles, and it will be a sorry day if the Liberal party has to learn its Liberalism from the socialists.
That comes from an editorial in the Free Press, the title of which is "The C.C.F. Shows Courage", and everyone knows that the Free Press does not go out of its way to hand compliments to the C.C.F. In this matter, however, they have carried on a consistent fight to have this business changed before parliament rises.
Do you always believe what the Winnipeg Free Press says?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Oh, no. More often than not it is wrong, but when it is right I do not mind saying so. Even the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) is right on occasion, and when he is I do not hesitate to say so. But not only are newspapers and

periodicals working on the matter. Organizations covering a wide range of public thought have been interesting themselves in this question. In this instance I have received communications from boards of trade and trade unions, and frequently when you get communications from these bodies they are on opposite sides of the fence. But this time they are on the same side. I have had communications from a number of church organizations. The United Church of Canada has been particularly active in the matter, and we have seen activity on the part of the National Inter-church Advisory Committee on the Resettlement of Japanese Canadians. This is headed by five of the largest Christian communions-the Roman Catholic archdiocese of Toronto, the United Church of Canada, Church of England social service, the Baptist convention of Ontario and Quebec, and the Presbyterian Church in Canada. All these people have written about this matter and have made representations to members of parliament and senators, and they feel exactly as we do about it, that what is really at stake is not what is happening to. a few individual Canadians of Japanese origin. What we are concerned about is maintaining in Canada, sound and undisturbed, the principle that the franchise is based upon humanity and that there should be no racial discrimination so far as the franchise is concerned. Documents that I have read from years gone by state the Liberal position. The Prime Minister has stated that position even as recently as the outbreak of this war, for during the war session of September, 1939, he expressed the hope that there would be no racial intolerance or bigotry during the period of the war, and he welcomed support along that line from the then leader of the opposition, the late Doctor Manion. The Prime Minister mentioned the fact that he himself had been born in a town which was known at that time as Berlin, Ontario; he referred to his own education in Germany, and he expressed the hope that we would maintain that genius of our Canadian democracy which is the ability to rise above any racial discrimination whatsoever.
Something has gone awry, and what we have before us now is not in keeping with the policy of the Liberal party. It is not in keeping with its traditions down through the years. I think a definite attempt should be made to correct this error, not simply for the sake of a few Canadians of Japanese origin but for own own sake, so that we may not descend to racial discrimination of any kind but keep ourselves a nation in which the highest principle is the principle of humanity.

Dominion Elections

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Hon. members should bear in mind the exact nature of the amendment and the side of the house from which it has been proposed. The amendment is intended to remove any possibility of racial discrimination with respect to the franchise and equally any possibility of racial favouritism. The amendment also, as I have said, has been moved by the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) who is a member of the government, and has made the motion he has on behalf of the government.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Knowles) might well have made the speech he has had the government been indifferent in this matter, and he were seeking to arouse its members to a remembrance of their past assertions and of their duties and obligations. But everything that he has said about the importance of not countenancing racial discrimination with regard to the franchise merely supports what this amendment is intended to effect.
Let me make it perfectly clear that, if this amendment carries, the position so far as this general election is concerned, in relation to Japanese, will be in practical terms what it would have been if clause 5 had never found a place in the bill. It leaves the matter of the right of voting on the part of the Japanese just where it would have been but for changes in the place of residence of some of them which have taken place as a consequence of the war.
I must take my share of credit or blame along with all my colleagues for anything that may have been done from this side of the house by way of omission or commission, to which exception may be taken. I therefore wish to say at once, what I believe was in the mind of the administration in having the amendment to the elections act proposed in the words it was by the insertion of section 5. It was to prevent the possibility of racial favouritism in the exercise of the franchise and of racial favouritism shown to members of the race whose country to-day is at war with our own.
Under clause 5 the right of all Japanese, even those not previously resident in British Columbia, would have been taken away, because that right is denied to Japanese resident in British Columbia. What would that mean? It would mean that the government was recognizing the franchise as existing in one particular province as being the one which should determine the franchise for the whole dominion. That is something that would not be entertained for a moment by
this house once the implication is apparent. Hon. members will ask, why was that not foreseen? The answer is very simple. The purpose of the bill as it went to the senate was to prevent Japanese who would not have had the right to vote had they remained in British Columbia from having that right in different parts of Canada simply because they had moved or had been moved from that province for reasons connected with the war. Let me make the position clear according to the facts. So far as the Japanese were concerned they had no right to exercise the franchise in British Columbia. Their citizenship was limited in that province; and for as long as I can remember where a province has had a franchise -that restricted for racial reasons the right of certain classes to vote in that province the dominion has with respect to federal elections taken cognizance of that fact as regards that province. But it has never held that what any province might do in the matter of the franchise in its own province should be made to govern the franchise as it would be exercised in other provinces of Canada.
What happened after Pearl Harbor? For purposes of security to the nation, particularly for purposes of security to British Columbia, this government arranged the transfer from British Columbia of large numbers of Japanese. It transferred these Japanese to different provinces. It did that, as I have said, as a measure of security. It was never intended by the government of Canada at the time that that step was taken that the Japanese who were being thus transferred would be given a right in a general election which they would not have had had they remained in British Columbia, or would give them a right which the Japanese remaining in British Columbia would not have in this election. The purpose of the bill was to remove any possibility of favouring that large number, but what was the effect of it? There was an effect which was not apparent to anyone at the time, or it would have been pointed out at once. It had the effect of taking away from the Japanese who were in provinces other than British Columbia a right which they would have had to vote as citizens of Canada in those provinces, and as such was in the nature of racial discrimination. By this amendment we are seeking to make it clear that such was never the intention of the government. It was never the intention to exercise racial discrimination. The intention was simply to prevent certain Japanese from being favoured in the matter of the exercise of their franchise in a manner which they would not have been but for the war. What

Dominion Elections
are the facts? Take the numbers that are concerned. The figures that I have are approximate, but prior to Pearl Harbor the 1941 census gives the number of Japanese who were outside of British Columbia as a thousand. Of that thousand less than 650 were twenty years of age or over. A large number of those were not naturalized; consequently the voting strength of the entire Japanese people outside British Columbia was negligible. In addition they were scattered throughout the dominion and for that reason their vote, if exercised, would not have been likely to affect one way or the other the result in any constituency.
This was the position that had to be dealt with. To prevent the thousands of Japanese who had moved or been moved out of British Columbia from voting at this election in other provinces some measure had to be taken to make it clear that they were not to have that right, and the bill as it was drafted was aimed at those particular Japanese. But, as I say, it overlooked the fact that in' the taking of that step there were a few in the other provinces who -were Canadian citizens who would have been disfranchised as a consequence. The best evidence that the government has held determinedly to this view that there shall be no racial discrimination as such in connection with the franchise is that at this moment we are proposing the amendment we are to the bill as it has come back to this house from the senate. I might mention one other matter. Had the large number of Japanese, those who had moved or been moved out of British Columbia, had the right to vote at an election where they would not have had that right had they remained in British Columbia I am pretty sure that had they sought to exercise it there might have been riots at some of the polls at the time of the election when Japanese presented themselves. It was exercising the part of wisdom to see that nothing of the kind should take place.
When the plebiscite bill was put through this house it contained a clause for the purpose of preventing the very possibility of riots arising because of the Japanese voting on the plebiscite. The clause was inserted in the bill and approved by this house and by the senate, by all parties in parliament, that they should not have the right to cast their votes in that plebiscite. It was done not for reasons of racial discrimination, it was done for purposes, if you like, of protection of the Japanese themselves. Instead of discriminating it is a means of saving them from possible injury that they might have suffered had they attempted to vote.
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
What has been done with respect to this measure was to have a clause inserted in the bill similar to that which was in the plebiscite bill and for precisely the same reasons; but the point that I wish to make clear at the moment is that the effect of this amendment is to prevent thousands of Japanese who are now in the different provinces of Canada, but who had been residing in British Columbia at the time of the war from having any right in the matter of the franchise which they would not have had had they remained in British Columbia at this time. I think the house will agree that we should not discriminate on racial lines at any time, but equally we should be doubly careful, and particularly at a time of war, not to give to those of a race with whose country we are at war rights which they would not have except for the exigencies of war itself.

In the light of all that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said about the government's determination to prevent the exercise of discrimination I think we should look at the clause we are amending. This bill must have had the approval of the cabinet before it was introduced into the house. It was introduced by a responsible member of the cabinet. As I understand it, the effect of the clause would have been to disfranchise at a federal election any group of people of alien race that had at the time of the election been disfranchised by any province. It did not refer to this particular war, but to any war in which Canada was engaged. Therefore it is quite obvious that it was the intent of the government, or certainly the intent of those who framed this bill, and the intent of those who sponsored this bill, that we should give over to the provinces the right to determine who should vote at a federal election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to
my hon. friend that I rose to make it perfectly clear what the intention was, and I made it perfectly clear that the intention was not to take away a right from any one who had the right but to see to it that rights were not given to persons who had not previously enjoyed them, particularly when they were of a race with whose country we are at war.
Perhaps instead of using the word "intent" I should have said the effect of this clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is why
the amendment is being introduced, to remove that effect, which was due entirely to an oversight on the part of hon. members on all sides, as is quite apparent this morning.

Dominion Elections

Certainly there was a storm of protest across the country, and an amendment was adopted in the other house which brought this bill back to the House of Commons. I am doubtful as to just how much credit the country will give the Liberal government for the reintroduction of this measure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are not
looking for credit. We are looking for justice, that is all.

That will remain to be seen. The amendment adopted by the senate would have the effect of disfranchising at a federal election only those who at the time of the passing of this act had been disfranchised by a provincial government, which in effect would mean the disfranchisement of all people of Japanese origin in Canada. The government has sought to patch up the evident mistake it made by inserting clause 5 in the bill in the first place, by easing the situation a little more and leaving the right to vote with those who were not resident in British Columbia before the war, the number of whom the Prime Minister indicated was very small. What he is doing now by the amendment introduced, and I think we must understand it, is this. Formerly a province had the right to determine who in that province would vote in a provincial or federal election. Now the government is making it possible for one province to determine not only who in that province shall vote in a federal election but who in all provinces may vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No; we are
doing the very opposite.

We have not a copy of the amendment, but is it not true that the effect of the amendment is to disfranchise the Japanese who were residing in British Columbia, whether at the time of the election they were residing in British Columbia or in any other province?
Yes, but it does not give the legislature the power to determine that now; the power must have been exercised six years ago. No fresh power is given.

But it does extend beyond the borders of British Columbia the provisions which that one province has made with regard to its electors. A number of statements have been made as to the circumstances under which the bill was introduced. The Prime Minister himself has admitted that there was an oversight on the part of some of the members of the government. The minister responsible has indicated that never was
desire for haste indicated by the government in connection with the passing of this bill, but on that occasion apparently a number of circumstances occurred which as far as I can remember have not occurred on any other occasion. To begin with, the bill was not printed and in the hands of hon. members until it was called for second reading. Then the assurance was given by the minister that schedule A followed the recommendations of the committee. It is true that the minister did not refer to the bill itself, and apparently no hon. member had the foresight to ask him if there was anything in the bill that had not come before the committee.
It was read clause by clause.

Clause 1 was read; then, according to Hansard for June 9, clauses 2 to 11 were called together. As far as I remember this is the only instance since I have been in this house when a bill has not been called clause by clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, what nonsense !
My recollection definitely is that every clause was called specifically. They were not carried en bloc in that manner.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend was in the house last week when the measure concerning national health and welfare was under discussion. Half a dozen clauses were called and put through without debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On a point -of order, Mr. Speaker, I was chairman of the committee, and I say here and now that the clauses were called one by one and the marginal notes read.
And Hansard proves it.
According to page 3692 of Hansard section 1 was agreed to. The next item is "Sections 2 to 12 agreed to." Then a discussion ensued.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Hansard may
record it in that manner, but the Deputy Speaker has just mentioned to my hon. friend that the marginal notes were called. Hansard does not put down everything that is called, but the word of the Deputy Speaker should be sufficient to answer the hon. gentleman.
In connection with that point of order I would direct attention to page 3696 of Hansard where I see, "Section S agreed to."

And the bill was before the house four days.
Dominion Elections

I am not excusing myself, Mr. Speaker; I have to take my share of blame along with other hon. members of the house. I am satisfied, however, that if hon. members had been given the opportunity of reading that bill clause by clause objection would have been raised to clause 5.
Mr. BRjADETTE : Again I must raise a point of order. The hon. gentleman is casting a reflection upon the Chair. I was chairman of that committee and never, at any time, have I tried to railroad any bill or any clause through. I am in the judgment of the committee as to the bill in question, but I repeat that every clause was called by itself and the marginal notes read. If the committee had asked me to read the clauses in full I would have done so gladly.

Reference was made to page 3696 of Hansard, where it is said that section 5 was agreed to. May I call the attention of the house to the fact that the section 5 there has reference to the schedule and not to the bill itself.

The provisions of the bill and the schedule were gone over, section by section. It does refer to the schedule. But the whole bill was gone over in the ordinary and regular way. The suggestion is that in some manner-and I do not know how-the bill was treated in an extraordinary fashion. So far as I am aware-and as Mr. Deputy Speaker has made clear-it was treated in the regular manner of a bill passing the house. If hon. members did not see it, of course -that is not our fault.
Apparently the hon. member is not the only one who did not see it.
Did I understand the hon. member to say the bill was not read section by section? Does he not accept the wordl of Mr. Deputy Speaker that it was dealt with in that way?
Let him withdraw.
Did I understand the hon. member to say it was not read section by section?-
Yes.
-and that the bill was not gone through in the regular way, as Mr. Deputy Speaker has intimated?
I was calling attention to the fact that Hansard reports that sections 2 to 12 were agreed to, en bloc.

I must point out that Hansard is only a record of the proceedings 
of the house, but it is not the official record. Mr. Deputy Speaker has called attention to a statement made by the hon. member, and has pointed out that the only inference which can be drawn from the hon. member's observations is that Mr. Deputy Speaker did not read the sections of the bill, when it was before the committee, and that in some way the bill was not properly before the committee. Does the hon. member wish to convey that meaning to the house?
No. My suggestion was that the bill received hurried consideration by members, including myself-

I would ask the hon.
member to withdraw any implication or inference that Mr. Deputy Speaker did not conduct the passage of the bill, when it was before the committee, in the ordinary fashion,, and the fashion in which he says it was conducted. I would ask the hon. member to make a withdrawal, and1 to make it clear, so that it may be recorded in Hansard, that there was no improper procedure on the part of Mr. Deputy Speaker.

I withdraw anything that may imply that the chairman of the committee was lax in his duty, or attempted to railroad anything through the house. I am putting the blame where I think it belongs- on myself, and on other members of the house.
I believe I can say that the government's amendment offered this morning is more generous than that proposed by the senate, and that both are more generous than the original section. Under those circumstances we shall have no choice but to support them, since Your Honour has ruled our subamendment out of order. But we still feel that the section is not sufficiently generous, and that there is still an element of discrimination on racial grounds, of which we believe this country does not approve.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put I should like to make my position clear to the house and to the many people who -have given me responsibility in this matter, and who look to me as a defender of democracy.
In the first place -may I congratulate the government upon the amendment brought in. May I concur in many statements of regret which have been made with respect to the events which took place when the bill was first before the house. I too am one of those who failed to catch the significance of this section. The reason I think is clear, and is

Dominion Elections
the fault of no one. It will be observed that section 5 of the bill has the effect of adding subsection (n) to section 14(2) of the act. To be clear on what the amendment really involved, it was necessary to read section 14(2). True, one could have looked at the explanation, and gained from it the meaning of the amendment. It was perfectly plain to anyone who looked at and considered it. But everyone who knows about the hulk of material which passes through this house, and is familiar with legislation, can understand how a section of this kind might pass without its effect being fully realized.
The effect of the section as it went to the senate was a threat to disfranchise all Canadian citizens whose racial origin was that of a country at war with Canada. It was a complete racial discrimination against Canadian citizens of Japanese origin. Fortunately the other house debated the bill and made some excellent changes. Unfortunately however the other house and the present amendment have not entirely satisfied my conscience.
There are two principles to which I think the Liberal party has always held firmly. One is against racial discrimination, and the other is that all members of the party shall be perfectly free to express themselves when fundamental and basic issues are at stake. In this instance I see these two things: I see, first, that the government has no intention of embarking upon legislation involving racial discrimination, and that apparently it believes the amendment now before the house accomplishes that purpose. Far be it from me to attempt to teach other members of the house the fundamental principles of liberalism, good government, racial equality and all that sort of thing. We are all agreed upon that.
At one oclock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I was making the observation that it was not for me to attempt to teach Liberalism or democracy to any other member of this house, and! particularly to the members of the government. The head of the government has been preaching and working for democracy even longer than I and under much greater difficulties and larger responsibilities. I said also that there were two main principles in Liberalism, the first being racial equality, and the second that complete freedom be accorded to all members of the party to express their views when fundamental and basic principles are at stake, 100-310
as in my judgment they are in this instance.
I am sure that all will accord me the liberty of saying what I feel it is my duty to say and what I am impelled by conscience to say.
The government thinks, and the government says it thinks that the amendment now before the house is in line with the great principle of racial equality. The Secretary of State has said that every one who had a vote will vote. If that were entirely so I would be satisfied; if I could be made to see that that is so, I would be satisfied. But is it so?
All Japanese in Ontario and other provinces, with the exception of British Columbia, who are British subjects and who are twenty-one years of age right now have the right to vote. All Japs who left British Columbia and came to Ontario at any time in the history of Canada, now have the right to vote in every province of Canada other than British Columbia. The Japs who stayed in British Columbia have now the potential right to vote in every other province so soon as they satisfy the requirements of residence, provided, of course, that they are British subjects. There are thus three classifications.
It is not necessary to argue the complicated details of these amendments and this section. The fact stands out, and nobody wishes to controvert it, that those rights which I have just mentioned are by this bill to be taken away. To my untutored mind, to my simple way of thinking, that is race discrimination, in regard to which I could not remain silent in this house and keep proper relationship with my own conscience and with my own constituents. It is not in keeping with my mandate from the constituents whom I represent, the people with whom I must live I hope for many years to come. It is not in keeping with the fact that I have to live with myself, I hope also, for many years to come.
What the government has done is to refrain from disfranchising those Japs now resident in all provinces other than British Columbia and who were not residents of British Columbia from the year 1938 to 1939.
