For that concession, and it is a great one, I am thankful. I will vote for this measure and I will vote for it gladly. When the amendment of the Secretary of State has been passed it cannot then be said, as it could have been said had his amendment not been brought in, that all Japanese in Canada who are British subjects are disfranchised upon racial grounds. All Japanese in Canada who otherwise are entitled to vote are not disfranchised upon racial grounds.
Putting it conversely, it can be said that certain Japs can vote in Canada notwithstanding their racial origin. If there is some

Dominion Elections

disfranchisement, it is limited, and for that I am thankful. But unfortunately it will be said, and it can be said if this bill becomes law, that some Japanese are disfranchised in Canada on grounds of racial origin, and this is so expressed in the law itself. It is that residue of disfranchisement that affects my mind in approaching this matter.
On the other hand, those who might take fright because they are members of a racial group which is a minority, should bear in mind that what we are doing now is no precedent. It in no way indicates what we may do upon some other occasion. It must be remembered that the situation arises partly because of a legislative accident and partly because we are in a time of war.
Personally I know very little about the Japanese. I lived in British Columbia many years before the Japaneses arrived. I remember clearly my associations with their great enemies the Chinese and I developed in those days as a child a certain affection for the Chinese which I have carried into my adult years. But, as I say, this was before the Japanese colony arrived and accordingly I know very little about them, as compared with members who come from British Columbia and who have voiced on many occasions, I think unfortunately, their intense antipathy. I bow my head to their superior knowledge in that regard.
I know little about the Japanesee, other than the reports that I have read of the horrors committed by the military clique of Japan; their absolute barbarity, their meanness, their unfitness to live among civilized mankind. There is nothing that can be said in this house denouncing the military clique or the military actions of Japan with which I will disagree. I know little about the Japanese as such, but I know a lot about democracy. It is unfortunate that this incident should have arisen. It is so utterly unnecessary and has placed 'on the spot those who stand for democracy and who would fight for her, who would give their very lives for sound principle. It has placed them in a position of defending democracy and of appearing to defend the Japanese. I know a lot about democracy, and I know that if you can disfranchise yellow men on racial grounds, other groups may be disfranchised in the same way for the same or other reasons. If you keep that up, it will not be long before Canada will be Hitlerized. In Germany they started with the Jews; then came labour, then liberals; after that it did not matter-democracy was a thing of the past. I am apprehensive when we

touch something which even smells of racial discrimination and I am ready to oppose it with everything I have.
I have received a telegram from the Board of Home Missions of the United Church of Canada. This is what it says:
On behalf Board of Home Missions United Church protest strongly against clause 5, subsection 2, bill 135, on the ground of disfranchisement of all Canadian citizens of Japanese race now in process of satisfactory resettlement outside of British Columbia. The resentment aroused among these thousands of Canadian citizens of Japanese race who know no other home and who had hoped to live and die in this country and who by this bill will be left without nationality will be shared by thousands of fair-minded Canadian citizens. Believe this undeserved disfranchisement of Canadian citizens will reflect on the honour of Canada long after the war has been won.
That is the end of the telegram. The writer continues:
We who have had to do with the Japanese Canadians for a number of years feel especially strongly about the injustice of this proposed amendment of the election act. We feel the Japanese Canadians are surely worthy of exactly the same treatment as the German Canadians and Italian Canadians. To penalize one group of Canadian citizens purely on the basis of race is to us undemocratic and unchristian.
I read from a communication from the national inter-church advisory committee:
It seems to us absolutely unfair to put upon the backs of these Canadian Japanese, particularly of the guiltless Canadian born young people among them, responsibility for the actions of the military clique in Tokyo. The majority of them have never seen Japan, they have been brought up and educated in Canada, and their life and loyalty are here.
Someone said from across the floor this morning that most of us belong to minority races. I should like to correct that. In Canada all of us belong to minority races, and even did we not, far be it from me to ever use a majority to deny to a minority its natural rights. I remember when I was a boy my father used to tell me, "Never hit a boy smaller than yourself, because", he said "he may grow". I have always felt that we in the province of Ontario who seem to enjoy a majority in Canada should be very careful indeed never to abuse that power of numbers, lest the others might grow. I could not face the minority groups in my own city-the Ukrainians, the Poles, yes the Italians, and many others-if I allowed this occasion to pass without making myself absolutely clear before this house and the country that, when it comes to racial discrimination of any kind against anybody, count me out.
In my humble opinion, expressed with deference to everyone else who looks at the matter in a slightly different light, there is only one

Dominion Elections
class who should be disfranchised in this country. I refer to men and women who are not British subjects. We never have, and we never will, extend our franchise to those who are not British subjects. So, Mr. Speaker, I shall move:
That there be inserted in clause 5, subsection 2(n), in the first line after the word "person" the following words, "not being a British subject".
You will observe that thereby the viciousness of the clause will be entirely eliminated, because then the franchise will be extended to British subjects who qualify by residence and age and other things of that kind, and will be denied only to those who are not British subjects. Anybody may second it who pleases. I have asked no one.
I would like very much to second that.

Paragraph (n) of subsection 2 would then read, "Every person not being a British subject residing in Canada whose racial origin" et cetera.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Battle-ford) : If I understand this amendment correctly, it is one of which I am in favour, and I shall give it my support. I think I am right in believing that its purpose is to give any Japanese citizen who is a British subject the right to vote in a federal election. The principle involved in this discussion to-day is one which appears to me to be so important that no hon. member can possibly forgo the opportunity of expressing himself on it or of taking sides on this issue.
In this federal house we cannot in any degree be responsible for laws or decisions made in the province of British Columbia, but definitely it is our duty to preserve an impartial judgment on all matters regarding the franchise in the federal field and see to it that the basic principles of democracy are not in jeopardy for one moment by any act or ruling of a provincial government. In war time the rights of minorities, the rights of people who happen to belong to a nation with whom we are at war, must be regarded more carefully than in times of peace.
Undoubtedly, in wartime, hysteria among our people is more easily aroused and can become very dangerous. Personally I am not concerned with the reason why the legislature of British Columbia has made such laws as it has with regard to the Japanese in that province. I am of the opinion that the feeling towards the Japanese did not originate at the beginning of this war. It did not have its basic causes in the fact that we are at war with Japan and that the people of British
Columbia feared action on the part of some Japanese nationals within their province. It is far more deepseated than that. The reason has its basis in the economy of that province. But I cannot help saying that I fail to see why this federal house should take the attitude that British Columbia still has the right to decide whether Japanese in the rest of Canada should vote in a federal election. First of all, who was it who wanted the Japanese removed from British Columbia? It was the people of that province and that government who made the request to the federal government that certain numbers of Japanese be removed from British Columbia. If that province no longer wanted the Japanese there, if they did not want responsibility for providing a livelihood for these people and having them thrown instead on the back of the federal government, by what right has the province of British Columbia now to say what shall be done with regard to these Japanese people outside their province voting in a federal election?
To-day the Japanese who are living in Canada outside British Columbia come under the jurisdiction, I believe, of the Minister of Labour. He was responsible for their removal, responsible for seeing that they had the means of livelihood, and therefore the government of British Columbia, in my opinion, loses all right to consideration on this question of the franchise of these Japanese people. She threw them outside, deprived them of the means of livelihood and refused responsibility for them in that respect, and now she wishes to exert rights over them in the matter of federal franchise. If the people of the province feel that way about it, I think that we in the federal house should assert our responsibility towards the Japanese and see that they are treated as any other people should be treated.
The people of British Columbia are the only ones who can decide what should be done with regard to the Japanese who remain within the borders of that province, but I would like to know if there is a federal member in this house to-day who has a mandate from his constituents to prevent any person-mind you, apart from those who are not British subjects, apart from those who are charged with sabotage of the war effort-from exercising the franchise in the federal field. I do not believe that any federal member has a mandate from his own people so to disregard the rights of a minority people in the federal field of franchise.
To support the amendment which has just been offered seems to me the only means of expressing the democratic rights of people within this country. The amendment made
Dominion Elections

by the Secretary of State still acknowledges the right of British Columbia to dictate regulations with regard to people whom she refuses to have within the borders of her own province, and I really cannot see how any federal member could possibly support such an idea. The number of Japanese citizens remaining in this country is quite considerable. I believe the figures from the Department of Labour are roughly these. There still remain in British Columbia, 15,733 of these Japanese, of whom 73 per cent are Canadian citizens. Outside British Columbia we have only about 4,835 in the prairie provinces, of whom 79 per cent are citizens of Canada, and in eastern Canada there are 3.065, of whom 81 per cent are Canadian citizens. Taking all those east of the Rocky mountains, there are roughly about 6,000, and of that number 4,000, I believe, have the right to vote. But it does not matter how many there are. Were there only 400, were there only 40 or only 4, the principle remains. It is a question of their rights as citizens.
I cannot see where these Japanese citizens are any different from the citizens of any other racial origin residing in any part of Canada. On what grounds can any member in this chamber dispute their right to vote? It seems to me that if British Columbia still wanted to exercise rights over her Japanese people she should have thought of this before throwing them outside the province and on the hands of the federal government. But once she has done that, I cannot see what right she still has in the question of their voting federally. It may be that this refusal of British Columbia to keep all her Japanese people within her borders will do great good to the Japanese, because as long as they were in that province the rest of Canada did not know much about them. Many of us took our opinions about them from what we heard from citizens of British Columbia; but since many of them have been removed and have gone into the prairie provinces and Ontario, the Canadian people are beginning to realize that it is not the colour of a man's skin that makes him a good or a bad citizen, but his training, his upbringing and the question whether he is proud and happy to belong, to Canada. Many of these Japanese who have gone to live in eastern Canada, as we read in manj' magazines to-day, have been accepted by the people among whom they live as decent, honest, fine citizens only willing and anxious to abide by the laws of this country and to do everything they can to make themselves like other Canadians.

Of course the Japanese are the same as any other of the peoples with whom we are at war. I believe we have had a few among them who have been charged with subversive activities. We have had some among the Germans and some among the Italians whom we have had to place in internment camps. We have also had a few hundred Japanese who have been placed in internment camps and naturally they would be debarred from voting. That would be a very natural thing for us all to agree to.- But do we debar either Germans or Italians in this country from the federal vote? Certainly not. As far as I know, even some of those Germans who have been in the internment camp because it is known that they did indulge in subversive activities, but who have since been released by the Minister of Justice, have the vote, and certainly hundreds of these Japanese are not in the same category. So that if we do not debar such German people from the vote, how can we possibly deny the vote to Japanese people who have never at any time given us the same cause or reason to believe that they would indulge in subversive activities in Canada?
The Prime Minister's argument. about Japanese going to the polls and getting mobbed was one of the weakest I have ever heard him put forward. He was afraid of allowing the Japanese the franchise because in going to the polls the rest of the people of Canada might mob them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Pardon me; I did not say anything of the kind. I indicated certain considerations that had to be taken into account, but I made no statement of my own to that effect.

I am sorry, but I must say that the Prime Minister left the impression with me that he thought that if some of the Japanese went to the polls to vote there might be little riots-I believe the word riot was actually used in that connection-at the polls.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I said that was a consideration that governed when the plebiscite bill passed this house and passed the house without any exception being taken to it. The clause to which exception is now being taken is, I think, a duplicate of that which appeared in the plebiscite bill.

Of course it is some
time since the plebiscite was taken, and I think a good many of us have a very different idea on these matters now from what we had at the time of the plebiscite. We have had

Dominion Elections
reason, to see how peaceful and quiet have been the Japanese who have been moved in to other parts of Canada. I realize that they voted in the Ontario election, and I certainly did not hear of any riots in the Ontario election on the part of people who did not like to see the Japanese going to the polls.
I see no reason to believe that in a federal election there would be anything of that kind. Perhaps at the time of the plebiscite it may have been in the minds of some people, but after all is said and done, even if we do fear that some of the Canadian people would not like to see the Japanese people going to the polls, in my opinion that would be no reason for preventing them. Mob violence has no place in a democratic country. Law-abiding Canadian citizens do not indulge in such things unless they are incited to do so by those who wish deliberately to promote race hatred. Race discrimination is a fascist trend which should have no place in our country. It should be guarded against by our police. We have federal and provincial police in this country to guard the rights of citizens, and if there was any fear that the rest of the people of Canada might indulge in little riots at the polls because Japanese people were going there to vote, then I would say it was our duty to protect the Japanese by seeing that the police were there to stop others from rioting. It would definitely be appeasing such fascist trends to deny the Japanese people the right to vote just because we think such a thing might happen.
So far as the police have been able to tell us, the Japanese people themselves have not been responsible for making any disturbances. I quote from the Vancouver News-Herald, of Monday, July 3, 1944, as follows:
Not a single act of sabotage has been attempted by any Japanese in this province since the outbreak of war with Japan, Deputy Commissioner John Shirras of the provincial police told the annual business conference of the Pacific Coast international association of law enforcement officials. Mr. Shirras spoke on "The Japanese Problem on the West Coast."
"It is a problem that requires care and tolerance," he said, criticizing persons who have "rushed into print" on Japanese matters.
"The public has been unnecessarily inflamed by such individuals," lie added. "The problem is an international one that cannot be dealt with by individuals."
I have already had occasion to speak in this house on what I considered to be the lack of democratic action within the department of the Secretary of State, particularly the selling of the property of the minority group of Ukrainians in this country. I consider that to be an outrage. I also consider it a wrong thing for the department of the
Secretary of State to dispose of the property of the Japanese people in this country, as has been done recently, and for sums of money that are not really anywhere sufficient to cover the cost of the buildings and property concerned. It has more or less resulted in giving this property away. I am very much against this kind of thing. I believe it is a tendency which we should be very willing to correct, and we should see that it does not happen again.
I certainly am against the idea of the army refusing to take Japanese soldiers. I see no reason why hundreds of these young Japanese men, physically fit and well, should not be allowed to go and fight, if they wish to, for the democratic ideals of this country where they were born and which they now call their home. How are we ever to make them into good Canadian citizens unless we give them a chance to fight and work for the things which they have been brought up to believe in, in our schools, colleges and universities? It seems that in the United States they are taking a very different attitude on this whole matter, and I am led to believe that we should be better off were we to follow in their footsteps. In the United States they have 12,000 young Japanese fighting in their armies. One group of roughly one thousand of them went into action in Italy. Numbers of them were wounded and as a result of their gallant fighting many medals and commendations were given to that particular regiment. The property of the Japanese people has not been sold in the United States, and that again is one more protection of their rights which I would like to have seen in this country. In the United States they seem more anxious to maintain the citizenship and the rights of their Japanese-Amerieans.
I should like to quote to the house a brief paragraph from a speech which was made by the Secretary of the Interior of the government of the United States, Mr. Harold Ickes, when he spoke at San Francisco on April 13, 1944, because his words are the words and the sentiments that I myself would like to have uttered. He said:
I hope that the clamour of those few among you who are screaming that this situation (i.e. the Jap American problem) should be resolved on the basis of prejudice and hate will soon be overwhelmed by the stern remonstrances of those among you-an overwhelming majority-who believe in fair play and decency, Christianity, in the principles of America, in the constitution of the United States. . . .
The War Relocation Authority-make no mistake about it-has been criticized for not engaging in this sort of lynching party. Under my jurisdiction, it will not be stampeded into undemocratic, bestial, inhuman action. It will not be converted into an instrument of revenge
Dominion Elections

or racial warfare. ... I am particularly grateful to those groups and individual on the west coast who have been brave enough and Christian enough to speak out against the vindictive,
bloodthirsty onslaught of professional race-mongers. ...
We must all face the problem of the eventual status and treatment of those Americans of Japanese descent who were taken from their homes and transported to evacuation camps. Most of them, after a thorough investigation, the doubts being resolved in favour of segregating them, have proved to be loyal and devoted to their nation (i.e. U.S.A.). It is intolerable to think that these people will be excluded from a normal life in this country for long. It is intolerable to think that merely because they resided on the west coast-in California, or Washington, or Oregon-they must be wards of the government for one moment longer than the necessities of the war require. I know of no virus in these three states which has infected them so that they must be treated differently from the Japanese Americans who reside in other states.
I should like to ask, Mr. Speaker, what virus has infected the Japanese who have remained in British Columbia and who have been recently brought out to the rest of Canada that makes them different from any Japanese who may have lived in Ontario or any other part of Canada since before the war? There is no difference in those people- none, whatever, so far as I can see.
The purpose of this amendment will, I believe, commend itself to hon. members of the house. I myself cannot agree to depriving any citizen of Canada of any right, believing that if I do so my own rights and the rights of future generations are thus jeopardized. The people who belong to the Japanese race who reside in other parts of Canada-who reside anywhere in Canada, I will go that far-are in my opinion innocent of any sabotage against Canada and Canada's war effort until they are proven guilty. On these grounds I believe that the fullest democracy should be granted to them. I cannot help but think that the government is making the jurisdiction of British Columbia rather an excuse for denying the rights to those Japanese people in other parts of Canada, and I cannot find myself in agreement with such an idea. I whole-heartedly support the amendment which has just been introduced.

I have been considering
the amendment which has been introduced. I am of the opinion it is not consequential. If any hon. member wishes to speak on it I shall be glad to hear him now.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
On the point of order which Your Honour suggested, may I say the effect of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) would be to confer the franchise
fMrs. Nielsen.]
not only upon Canadian bom who have left the province of British Columbia but actually upon those who are still in British Columbia. I submit that it is not relevant to the bill as it passed this house on third reading, nor is it consequential upon the amendment as introduced by the other house, and therefore it is distinctly out of order.
Does any other hon. member wish to speak to the point of order?

As to the question of the constitutionality of the amendment I should like to make one point. I take issue with the minister in his statement that the amendment I have placed in Your Honour's hands would extend the franchise to the Japanese of British Columbia. As I read the act and the amendments before us. that is not so. I direct attention to chapter 46 of the statutes of Canada, 1938. Section 14, subsection 2 reads:
The following persons are disqualified from voting at an election and incapable of being registered as electors and shall not vote nor be so registered, that is to say-
This is the paragraph in question:
(i) every person who is disqualified by reason of race from voting at an election of a member of the legislative assembly of the province in which he or she resides and who did not serve in the military, naval or air forces of Canada in the war of 1914-18.
That clause is not affected by the amendments contained in bill No. 135, so that irrespective of what we do with regard to the senate amendments or with regard to section 5 of the bill, paragraph (i) of subsection 2 of section 14 still stands. I should like to make it perfectly clear that I am not arguing in favour of that section. I think the principle I have stated should also apply to that section, but it is not before the house. The principle stands as I have stated it, but from a legal point of view the fact remains that the minister must have overlooked this subsection. '

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is another point, in addition to the question I raised, that of whether this is a consequential or relevant amendment. The additional effect just mentioned by the hon. member for Trinity makes the amendment now moved ridiculous, because you would have two sections in the Dominion Elections Act of 1938 completely contradicting each other. That is the effect of the amendment now being moved.

The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) referred to section 14 of the 1938 act, saying that his amendment would

Dominion Elections
not affect it and that it would still remain in force. Let us read what is proposed in section 5 of this bill. It refers to subsection 2 of section 14 of the said act," which is the act of 1938, which I have in my hand and which the hon. gentleman says is not affected. That is the very section. It is idle to say that it is not affected. I entirely agree with the statement of the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
I did not say that. I said it did not affect paragraph (i) of that section.

Well, that is part of the section; that is a paragraph of subsection 2. The principle of amending is set out in citation 589 of Beauchesne, which says an amendment must be relevant or consequential. This amendment is neither.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As a matter of fact two points of order have been raised by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, though he regarded one as more important than the other. The first point was as to inconsistency between the amendment moved by the hon. member for Trinity and the other sections of the bill. In that connection I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Trinity. It seems to me that the limitation on the disqualification which the hon. member for Trinity would write into paragraph (n) would apply only within the terms of paragraph (n) and would not-affeet the other paragraph referred to.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It destroys the other paragraph.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As to the other point, it seems to me that if the words inserted by the Jion. member for Trinity had been inserted as an amendment to the senate amendment they would have come within the senate amendment and would have been consequential. I offer this suggestion to the hon. member for Trinity if his amendment should be ruled out of order.

As I indicated when inviting the opinions of hon. members, I was of the opinion that the amendment offered by the hon. member for Trinity whs not -consequential upon the amendment moved by the senate. It imports something which was not dealt with by the senate amendment. That amendment dealt with the question of the time of disqualification. The amendment of the Secretary of State was intended to clarify a section which might be ambiguous. As I say, the amendment offered by the hon. member for Trinity has broadened the scope of the senate amendment, and introduced a new principle into both the senate amendment and the bill itself, which has been discussed by the house on third reading. In my opinion the scope of the amendment so broadens it that it is not consequential to the senate amendment, and I therefore rule it out of order.
Mr. Speaker-

I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has spoken on the bill and Your Honour has given a ruling on the point of order. Now the hon. member cannot speak on the point of order, and he, is out^ of order in rising to speak again on the motion for second reading.
I do not think my hon. friend knows what I am going to say.
I do not care what the hon. gentleman is going to say. He is out of order in rising to speak again on this bill.
Surely the Chair will hear what I wish clarified. One of the previous speakers suggested that my amendment would have been in order-
I would ask for a ruling on my point of order.
If the hon. gentleman insists upon it, I have given my ruling and 1 am not likely to change my mind.
I am not asking that you change your mind. I am asking for clarification.
Order.
The hon. member must resume his seat.
Is it necessary that 1 move-
I rise to a point of order. The hon. member for Trinity should take his seat.

I have considered what the hon. gentleman had to say. I have given it very careful consideration and have come to the conclusion which I have announced. Having given a ruling I cannot allow any discussion of it.

If no one else has a point of order to raise 1 should like to make a few remarks. I have listened patiently all day to ladies and gentlemen from parts of Canada other than British Columbia talk on a subject which is vital to British Columbia and on which the people of British Columbia surely should be best informed. I have offered no objection
Dominion Elections

to their lack of knowledge of the subject, though their ignorance was as pitiful as it was profound, but now perhaps it might be well for the country and the house to have at least some of the facts made known. The hon. member for Battle River will excuse me if I do not follow her argument, because our seats are so far apart, and I have an infirmity in my hearing, that I could not follow all she said.
I would like to contradict that. The lady is not from Battle River. Her constituency is North Battleford.

I beg the pardon of both hon. members. I trust I would be too gallant to criticize her remarks. But the hon. member for Trinity is more on my level, and I hope I may be able to answer some of his remarks.
I am sorry that' through rotten draftsmanship this trouble has been imposed upon the house. I am no lawyer, but I am told that this matter was in the hands of a committee of fifteen capable men, who sat at a number of sittings. I believe it is ten or twelve years since I have been given the opportunity to sit on any of these special committees appointed by the government. Probably they think I do not know enough about the situation-or perchance that I know too much. But I do know that if I had been on that committee I would have at least striven-I might not have succeeded-to avoid the horrible mess we have before us to-day.
This business passed the lawyers of the senate and the House of Commons, and I do not suppose there are three men who could state what the latest and1 best amendment is, after so much confusion. If I understood the hon. member for Trinity correctly, he said that the Japanese could vote in British Columbia. Well, that is such a stupendous departure from fact that I do not know where to begin, so perhaps I had better give a little sketch of the situation.
It is often said that it was the C.P.R. who brought them all in.
That is bunk. What happened is this: Possibly the Chinese were brought in to build the C.P.R., but it was not the Japanese at all. They were put on the voters' lists in some by-election-I think it was one in Cariboo. Some enterprising politician had filled the list with Chinamen and Indians. In 1875 in British Columbia they passed a law by which all Indians and Chinamen were struck off the voters' list. That was that.
Then the Japanese began to immigrate, and in 1895 the local legislature added the Japanese to the prohibited list which were not to be put on the voters' lists. Then the question came up as to the dominion franchise. 
This question does not appear in our dominion statutes until 1919, and for that reason some people argue the prohibition did not begin until then. But that is not right. The right way of it is this: Prior to 1919, I do not know just how far back, but probably about the time of confederation, the dominion government had a system in connection with the dominion franchise of adopting provincial voters' lists. Therefore this question of our making the dominion franchise never arose at all, because the dominion just took the provincial voters' lists. And as we took these voters' lists they never contained Japanese or Indians, because they had been struck off. It was only in 1919 that that'was necessary.
And, by the way, there is a point there I might just put in, because it is often alleged [DOT]-"Oh, these poor Japanese, coming here with their hearts bleeding with the desire to vote, the same as we do. The w'hite man is allowed to vote, but they are not allowed this priceless privilege." Pure bunkum! There was a discussion in committee some years ago in connection with voting, as to whether we should not compel the white man to take advantage of this "priceless privilege".
A delegation of Japanese came to Ottawa some years ago and appeared before a committee of the House of Commons which was dealing with the franchise. They were very capable people. One was a professor, one a dentist and another a schoolteacher. I do not remember what the fourth was, but I do remember they were able and cultured people-far better educated than I was, because I never saw the inside of a high school let alone a college. However we were allowed to ask them questions. At this point may I say that the Japanese has a very peculiar mentality. When he gets his piece off by heart, he will make a good yarn of it. But if he is confronted with an unexpected question he will probably break off and tell you the truth. We cross-examined them, and they gave us their story, and then we asked them some questions-the one to which I have just referred. We asked them when the Japanese were prohibited. The witness said, "Well, it never applied to us, because we were prohibited before ever we came here." I said, "Well, you were aware that those were the conditions to which you were coming when you came here?" And he said, "Yes".. So that all this sob story about the poor Japanese being deprived of their rights is all bunk. They knew the conditions which existed, just as one hon. member pointed out the other day in connection with our indemnities. We knew what we were taking when we took

Dominion Elections
the job; and the same applies to the Japanese., because they knew perfectly well that the law was against them. So that they are not being deprived of anything they ever had.
I was going to mention the dominion franchise. In 1919 the dominion government adopted a different method of making up the voters' lists. Instead of taking the British Columbia list, or the provincial lists, they made special lists. A registrar was appointed and he was compelled to make a list of all who were qualified in a certain area. Then it was necessary to do something about these prohibitions. It was in 1919 that the government of the day enacted into law the words which have remained ever since, and which I believe the hon. member for Trinity quoted from the 1938 statutes. It said that where a body of people on account of its racial origin was excluded from the provincial franchise, that prohibition would be carried on into the dominion franchise in that province. That became established in 1919, and it has been carried on since then. They never had the vote. They never were promised it, and never had the possibility of having it. That is how it comes that there is this connection between the dominion and the provinces. That was the way it was in 1919, and it has been continued year after year, with this same prohibition.
This thing which has been started up is all for political effect. It is not as though they were suddenly deprived of a privilege, because the Japanese never had a vote in British Columbia. At least it has been this way since 1895, so far as the Japanese are concerned, and since 1875 in connection with the Chinese and Indians.
The hon. member for Trinity admitted quite frankly-and I give him credit for it-that he knew very little about the Japanese and the situation in British Columbia. He told us that frankly. He said he knew a whole lot about democracy. Quite so; and I am pleased to listen to him when he discusses something about which he is so well informed. But would it not be a good idea to let those who do know what they are talking about deal with the situation in British Columbia? I am the first member who has stood in his place to-day-the first of sixteen members, to express the views of that part of the country from which we come, and with which we are thoroughly familiar. Does the hon. member not think it would be a good idea to give us just a little extra weight in the debate, because we know local conditions?
My hon. friend from Trinity said he had received a telegram, I believe it was, from a
church body, protesting against this legislation. Probably they sent a circular around to all the members some weeks ago.
Yes.

I know one member-it was not myself-who wrote back and said, "I have received your letter; it is clear you do not know the first thing about what you are talking about. Yours truly." I was more courteous, and went into a little more detail. However, the principle was exactly the same. I expressed regrets that the head of the church to which I belonged would squander our money in putting out Japanese propaganda- because it is nothing else. It drew a picture of the beautiful conditions under which some Japanese family had been discovered in Ontario, and it was written up to a fare-thee-well-the nice, respectable man, and the ladylike woman with the humble aspect, and the beautiful children, and all the rest of it! This circular said, "We appeal, we the people at the head of our church and your church and all churches appeal."
Not mine; mine was not in it.
You must be a Unitarian.
I am a Lutheran.

You can thank God that you belong to such a church. I expressed regret that I was paying out good money to subscribe to a church that was used for that purpose. They got out the circular and they appealed to the people in Ontario and Quebec, people who did not know the conditions in British Columbia along these lines, to take care of these people who were God's chosen people. They were asked to take them into their homes at a time when our men are being massacred and murdered by them in foreign lands. Our people were asked to take them into their homes and get them jobs because they are God's chosen people.
God's chosen people! The Japanese government held a convention, or whatever you call it, several years ago in connection with religion. They tried to decide what would be the most profitable religion to adopt because there was some talk that the old religion was getting a little threadbare and it might be a good thing to tie up with the other nations and adopt some other religion. They discussed the matter and they decided that the most profitable thing to do was to continue with the old Shinto religion because that would be the most profitable to the ruling class. Under that religion the emperor was the god and it was a beautiful thing
Dominion Elections

because in war time men could be made to believe that if they were killed they would go to the heaven of which their emperor was the god. They would prefer that to being taken prisoner.
These people are being moved out of British Columbia and they are being spread all over Canada like the smallpox disease. They will create little centres and groups of heathens in Ontario, Manitoba and so on. They will not fit in with their Christian surroundings because it is a set policy of the Japanese government to foment that religion. They must belong to it. Some of them have left British Columbia and they will create little propagandist centres for their pagan religion all over Canada. I suggested to these people who sent me these letters that that is not what we paid our good money for in preparing missionaries. We have been sending them to Japan but we could save a lot of money by having them try to convert these people at home. We could send these missionaries to Toronto or Montreal as the case may be and it would save considerable money. They are simply setting up propaganda centres for the spread of heathenism.
If I could take the time I could describe conditions in British Columbia that would make your hair stand on end-that is those of you who have sufficient hair to stand on end. I have never seen members from British Columbia pro-Japanese, but yes-I must be fair and say that there is one member from British Columbia who is at present in Australia. He was elected by the C.C.F. and all the time, in season and out of season, he loyally supports his Japanese, shall I say connections, or whatever it is; I do not know. The late Mr. Woodsworth, who used to sit down near where our friends are sitting now- the Minister of Pensions and National Health will bear me out in this-once said in connection with some bill that he believed in giving the Japanese votes. I asked him if he said that in the last election and he said, "Yes, and I will say it in any election." My friend opposite said, "Is that the view of the C.C.F.?" and he said, "Yes, that is the view of the C.C.F. as a body."
I know the hon, member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) said last year that that was still his view and that he would not continue to be a member of the C.C.F. if that view did not prevail. Of course that was a statement by a party. It was a small party, although it has grown smaller since then. It had seventeen members then, and now it has only ten. Naturally that attracted attention and I have no doubt it was wired to Tokyo that night. Inside of three or four

weeks that gentleman and his wife sailed for Japan on a Japanese vessel and I have no doubt that they treated him well while he was there. On his return he had hardly set his feet on the wharf at Vancouver before he was asking for votes for his brown friends and) so on. I leave that nasty insinuation; you can take it as you like. It is bad politics. There are few politicians in British Columbia who are willing-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order.
Thank you, I will have a rest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I speak on behalf of a member of this house who, as Your Honour knows, is absent because of the visit of the empire parliamentary association to Australia. If I heard the present speaker correctly he described something he said against the hon. member for Vancouver East as a nasty insinuation. I suggest if that is so, that it should be withdrawn.

I think my hon. friend's point is well taken. I did not say anything about him, I said it was I who was making a nasty insinuation. If you think that I should not have called1 it that, I will withdraw.
I think the hon. member's reference was to the late Mr. Woodsworth and not to the member for Vancouver East,

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I thought that was the case, and I thank the hon. member for New Westminster for his correction.

I never argue with the Speaker no matter what my -private opinion may be. But he has not pronounced anything so I think I may continue my brief rambling remarks. In fact I had finished. I could go on for another four or five hours and attempt to draw the true picture. I agree it is natural that eastern men cannot get the viewpoint we have in British Columbia. I am sorry that more weight is not given to the views of those who live in British Columbia and know what they are talking about.
The amendment before the house is simply an attempt to pacify, to remove the possibility of some injustice being done to people in the east. I thought the amendment suggested by the senate was sufficient, but the government in their wisdom have proposed an amendment which sounds a little more intricate. I will not say what is wrong with it because I do not understand it sufficiently. But I do hope we shall not have any more amendments like the one we had this morning which just added the words, "and when" or like the one this afternoon which has been ruled out of order.

Some kind friend placed a copy of the United Church Observer on my desk. It contains a picture of Mr. and Mrs. Umehara and daughter Millie in their farm home. I read most of it and really it would make your heart bleed. I am not attacking the Japanese.
I have met some decent Japanese and no doubt some of them would be loyal. But if you put five tons of potatoes in your cellar in the fall and you find many of them rotten in the spring, how can you tell which is which? You must say to these people, "We are sorry, you may not be all you are depicted to be, but we cannot tell, and the innocent must suffer for the guilty." This is a white man's country and we want it left a white man's country.
I suggest that we cannot accept amendments to this amendment unless they are shown to be consequential, and no one as yet has shown me the consequentiality of this one.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) has suggested that the people from other provinces should be prepared to listen to British Columbia opinion because the people there are so much closer to the situation. But I think he will understand that it is very hard for hon. members at this end of the chamber to hear everything that is being said at the other end. I think he will also agree that, while people from other provinces should be prepared to listen to what is being said by members from British Columbia, nevertheless the decision should surely rest with a province whether or not citizens resident within its boundaries should be disfranchised, and the people of British Columbia should not expect any other province to bow to their decision in that regard.
You ask us to do it with social credit.

I did not catch what the hon. member said. The amendment before the house undoubtedly removes many of the objectionable features of paragraph (n); nevertheless racial discrimination will still exist as a result of it; we shall still have a condition whereby the laws of one province will dominate the actions of certain Canadian citizens in other provinces, that is to say, Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry who were residing in British Columbia at the time of the declaration of war and who have removed to other provinces will still be subjected to the laws of British Columbia rather than of the province in which they reside. Therefore as a
result of this amendment we shall continue to have a violation of the rights of minorities on racial grounds.
In my opinion no loyal citizen of Canada should be debarred from exercising his responsibilities as a citizen merely because of his ancestry; and that, it seems to me, is the situation which will exist as a result of this amendment.	I understand that a number of
Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry and Japanese nationals were interned on the ground of subversive action at the start of the war; on the other hand, I understand that none of these Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry who have been moved have been guilty of any acts of sabotage since the war started.	I understand that in the various
provinces to which these people moved their record has been exceedingly good. We have had statements from the Minister of Labour giving us a very favourable record in that regard. I believe several hundreds of these Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry have attempted to enlist in the Canadian army and have been refused, and I think that is a pity, because no doubt they could have been of tremendous value. I recall that during the last war we had Canadian citizens of German ancestry in the army fighting against the Germans, and these men were of tremendous value because they had a thorough knowledge of the language and could be used to advantage. I understand also that some twelve thousand people of Japanese ancestry have been enlisted in the United States army; and surely if good use of them can be made there, we could make similar use of them in the Canadian forces.
We are not fighting to-day merely to defeat Germany and Japan; we are fighting in defence of definite principles. We are fighting for a peace based on justice, and justice must be granted to minorities as well as to majorities. It seems to me that this legislation is a negation of the declaration of principles contained in the Atlantic charter and accepted at Teheran.
I cannot understand, either, why we should single out Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry, why this is not applicable also to Germans and Italians. In saying that I do not suggest for one moment that it should be applied to either of those races; I am opposing the idea of making it applicable to Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry or any other. Once we start enacting discriminatory racial legislation of this kind it is very hard to know just where we shall stop. In view of the tremendous sacrifices which are being made to-day we cannot afford to make mistakes of this kind which may have such serious con-

sequences in the future. The cost will be too great. I am sorry that the amendment moved . by the hon. member for Trinity has not been allowed.

In anything I may say I shall be only echoing the remarks so well made by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck). I do not hold any particular brief for the Japanese; in fact, I do not see how anyone can, after the atrocities, of which one has read, that have been committed by them in this war. But to me the matter transcends considerations of race. It is a discriminatory act against one particular race of people; and, like speakers who have preceded me, I do not see how, if you penalize the Japanese in this matter, you leave the way open to discriminate against Hungarians, Bulgarians, Roumanians or other racial groups in the same way who are at present our enemies.
I see in this proposal a great danger to our entire democratic system. We pride ourselves on being an enlightened people, but by this discriminatory action we are trying to make a right by committing a wrong. It is not that I am without sympathy with the position of hon. members from British Columbia. I lived as a child for four years on the Pacific coast, in the state of California, and I know that people on the Pacific coast have a good case. At the same time are we, by singling out the Japanese for this kind of treatment, helping to make those who are naturalized or are second or even third generation Japanese, good Canadian citizens? Are we showing them the light of democracy and trying to get them to break away from old principles of the Samurai? I do not think so. I believe that by denying the vote to the Japanese outside-I repeat, "outside"-the province of British Columbia, who have migrated to other provinces since the outbreak of war on Japan, you are actually driving them back to old and alien principles which may have been instilled into them. In other words, instead of guiding them to enlightened citizenship and enabling them to realize their duties and responsibilities to Canada, you are encouraging them to revert to emperor-worship, to the code of Hirohito.
I strongly condemn any act or subclause of an act which discriminates in any way against the Japanese as a race, not only because I think we are thereby defeating our own purpose, but we are setting up a dangerous precedent by depriving British subjects of the rights to which they are entitled under the laws of the Dominion of Canada as a member of the British commonwealth of nations.
Would the hon. member allow a question?
Yes.

Is he aware that the Japanese have a dual nationality? They remain Japanese, yet have all the advantages of being British subjects; and they do not assimilate with us. That is why we put them in a different class from Germans and Italians.

Perhaps I was not very clear in what I was trying to say. I say they will continue to have a dual nationality so long as you discriminate against them. What we should do in this country is to try to lead them away from having a dual nationality, and make Canadians of them.

It is not my intention to take up very much of the time of the committee. I believe that hon. members of our group who have already spoken have made it clear that what we are fighting is not the matter of whether the Japanese shall vote or not; it is the principle underlying this bill, whereby the franchise of certain minority groups in this country is being curtailed, to which we are opposed. That it happens to be the Japanese who are the particular group is merely an accident. It might be any other group, as stated by the member who has taken his seat.
The Prime Minister states that what the government wishes to do is to see that there is no extension of the franchise at this time to any enemy aliens. To do this, it seems to me, he is accepting the principle that because one province disfranchises a certain group of people that disfranchisement shall follow those people into some other province and prevent them from voting at the next federal election in the particular province in which they may then happen to reside. What the Prime Minister is doing is not to prevent the extension of the franchise but to accept a new principle, which means a direct curtailment of the rights of the franchise, and he is using the fact that one province has already done this as a screen to hide behind.

The hon. member rather indicates that it is a new principle. I think he will agree that it is a principle that has been generally followed in section 14 of the general election act, to which clause 5 constitutes an amendment in the recognition of provincial limitations.

It does not follow in the election act that because one province disfranchises a certain group of people, those people are therefore disfranchised in any other

Dominion Elections
province. But that is what this bill does. It accepts the principle that because this particular group of people are disfranchised in British Columbia now, they shall be disfranchised in other provinces.
We accepted that principle in subsection (k) of section 14 of the election act, the same thing exactly.
No. I cannot agree with the Secretary of State. We are accepting it in this bill, but it has not been a principle that has been in force in Canada until this time.
It was included in the election act.

The Japanese in British Columbia have been disfranchised. It was within the right of that province so to do. I am not arguing their rights in that matter. But because they did that, it does not follow that the Japanese should be disfranchised in any other province. These people have moved from British Columbia to other provinces and have come under the jurisdiction of these other provinces and automatically they should obtain the franchise in those provinces unless this bill is passed in the form in which we have it at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The persons of whom my hon. friend is speaking are still citizens of British Columbia. They have moved or been moved from British Columbia temporarily for reasons connected1 with the war. They have been moved through arrangements effected by the government as a war measure which was deemed necessary for reasons of security and in part for the protection of these very Japanese themselves. In most cases they are not persons who have voluntarily left British Columbia to reside in some other province. They are still citizens of British Columbia.

Some of these people did automatically leave British Columbia themselves when this question arose. They moved to other provinoes without waiting for the government to move them, and they are being automatically disfranchised along with the others whom the Prime Minister states the government moved1, and who are now residing elsewhere. These people themselves moved to these provinces and1 by vrtue of residence in those provinces for a certain length of time they automatically become eligible to vote therein. I do not think the Prime Minister's arguments are sound, because ordinarily if these people had moved to a province and were Canadian citizens they would have the
vote automatically. Section 5, however, prevents this. It prevents the Japaneses in other provinces from voting, or it did before the senate amendment. The government amendment simply allows Japanese who were Canadian citizens and living in other provinces than British Columbia * prior to the war, to vote, but prevents Japanese Canadians who have been moved from voting.
Would the other provinces of Canada have accepted the Japanese if they had not been requested by the government to do so?

As far as I know, the other provinces had no laws on their statute books preventing Japanese from entering their boundaries. They never had any law on the statute books to that effect. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) moved an amendment which we believed would change the effect of this bill, but you, Mr. Speaker, did not accept that amendment for the reason that it changed section 5 of the original bill. We propose to move a further amendment which will be a consequential amendment in that it simply changes the time factor in the amendment to the amendment. It does not change the amendment except with respect to time. The amendment we now propose is this:
That the words "at the time of the passing of this act'', namely "July 1, 1938, and on the date of the declaration of such war resided" be deleted from the amendment and the following words substituted therefor:
"At a time subsequent to the next general election resides":
Also that where the words "on those dates" appear substitute "at that time".
Also for "was disqualified" read "is disqualified".

If the hon. member wishes to speak to his amendment I shall be glad to hear him, but I would ask him to address himself to this question. The amendment as moved by the Secretary of State deals with persons who are disqualified, and in the amendment which he is now proposing the hon. gentleman is disqualifying all persons except in relation to a later date, " subsequent to the next general election." I am afraid the hon. member has not seen the implications of the amendment. He would disqualify all at the next general election and entitle them to vote at a subsequent general election. If the hon. gentleman himself wishes to speak to the amendment, or if any other hon. membel wishes to do so;, I shall be glad to hear what is said.

speechtext: Is there a point of order, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, if you understood the motion that I made, I do not think you would rule it out of order. It simply changes the date of the coming into effect of a particular section of the act until after the next general federal election. It does not change the qualifications or disqualify anyone who was qualified to vote. All it does is to change the time of the coming into effect. Individuals affected will still be disqualified after the next general election, as they would be under this act in its present form. All this does is to say that prior to the next general federal election these individuals shall not be disqualified. It simply changes the time factor. It will be further changed by section 11 of the act. Section 5 will then go in its place, and it will automatically die with the ending of the war, but it will not change the qualifications of the voters. It will simply postpone the time of the coming into effect of certain disqualifications. These will not come into effect until after the next general election and will die six months after the war, according to section 11. Because it only changes the time factor it is a consequential amendment and therefore can be accepted. If it changed the qualifications of the individuals who could vote, then I consider Your Honour would be perfectly justified in ruling it out. But where it is a consequential motion and changes only the time factor, I respectfully submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that it can be accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
On the point of order, I submit that there is no difference whatsoever in principle between this amendment and the one that Your

Honour ruled out of order some time ago. In the second place I submit that not only does this amendment seek to do certain things by a question of time; the effect of the amendment that is sought is this: it changes the whole principle of this bill. It changes the whole principle of the bill which passed third reading in this house; it changes the principle of the amendment that came back io us from the other place, and therefore is not relevant. Certainly it is not consequential. It is the direct opposite to the principle of this bill. It means that these people are going to vote after the next general election, and after that they can be disqualified. Apart from the point of order, this is the most unethical amendment that I ever heard moved in this house.

After reading this amendment I have grave doubts as to its relevancy as being consequential to the amendments made by the senate. Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, paragraph 589, reads as follows:
When a bill is returned from the senate with amendments, the amendments are read and agreed to, or 'agreed to with consequential amendments, or disagreed to, or the further consideration thereof put off for three or six months, or the bill ordered to be laid aside.
No amendment can be proposed to the senate's amendment save an amendment strictly relevant thereto; nor can an amendment be moved to the bill, unless the amendment be relevant to or consequent upon either the acceptance or the rejection of a senate amendment.
I must come to the conclusion that the amendment submitted by the hon. gentleman is not consequential upon the amendments that have been made by the senate. I think I pointed ouh-
Pardon me. May I point out that my amendment is an amendment to the amendment submitted by the Secretary of State; it is not an amendment to the senate amendment.

We are dealing with the senate amendment which the Secretary of State has accepted, with an addition to it and therefore consequential to it; but in the amendment the hon. gentleman has submitted he is postponing the date of the disqualification to a period in the future, which is subsequent to the next general election. The principle that he is placing in the amendment is one which was not dealt with by the senate or by this house when the bill was before it. I must rule unhesitatingly that it is not consequential and therefore out of order.
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

There is one other matter about which I should like to ask a question at this point. I think I shall be understood perfectly when I say that I have no axe to grind, nor has any basic principle been violated, as far as I am concerned. However, something has occurred here to which it seems to me one might call attention more easily in connection with this bill than in some other cases. In view of the experience in connection with the bill with which we have just dealt, members of the government will perhaps appreciate that we are combing through the. bills much more closely than before. When the resolution preceding this bill was introduced on Friday last it read:
That it is expedient to amend the Salaries Act to provide that the salaries of the Minister of Veterans' Affairs and of the Minister of Reconstruction shall be ten thousand dollars, respectively.
That is all that was in the resolution, and on the basis of that resolution the bill to be introduced was to provide for two points, salaries for two ministers. When I received the bill in my mail on Saturday morning at first I thought it was the wrong bill, but when I looked it over I discovered that it contained six provisions instead of the two mentioned in the resolution. Those six provisions are: the two salaries named, the salary for the Minister of National Health and Welfare, a provision that the salary of the Minister of Pensions and National Health shall continue at the rate of $10,000 as long as he occupies that office and two other provisions which change the Minister of Railways and Canals to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of the Interior to the Minister of Mines
and Resources. There is nothing wrong in any of these changes, nor is there anything we did not expect or anything that should not have been done. It did strike me as strange, however, when we looked over the bill, to discover that on the basis of a simple two-point resolution we were presented with a six-point bill.
I only hope that in the dying days of the session the bills will conform a little more closely to the resolutions that are introduced.

Let me explain to my hon. friend. The law clerks who have to do with the drafting of these bills every now and then, when the opportunity occurs, take advantage of the chance to do what they call a little tidying up; that is to say, they bring up to date in one bill changes that have taken place in previous years but which have not been noted in that particular legislation. The designation of the portfolios of two or three of the ministry have been changed. For example, there used to be a Minister of Railways and Canals. His portfolio was changed to that of Minister of Transport. Since the Salaries Act lists several ministers my hon. friend will see cited the Minister of Transport, but he will not find anywhere in the list mention of a Minister of Railways and Canals. Attention is drawn to these changes in the explanatory note; it explains everything. As will be seen there, the person who was known formerly as the Minister of Railways and Canals to-day does not receive a salary under that designation; he receives his salary as Minister of Transport. The same is true with regard to the Minister of Mines and Resources, who was known previously as the Minister of the Interior. When the bill creating the Department of Mines and Resources was introduced it stipulated that this name should be substituted for that of Minister of the Interior. Previously the new minister had been drawing his salary as Minister of the Interior. After that bill was enacted the minister drew his salary, and is drawing it to-day, as Minister of Mines and Resources. So that no additional money is being voted in connection with those two ministers. To-day a salary is voted for the Minister of Pensions and National Health; I am happy to say that my hon. friend to my left has been getting his salary under that designation. However, we
Salaries Act

have created a new Department of Veterans' Affairs, which takes away part of the scope of the department of pensions and health. We have also put through this house, and I have no doubt it will pass the other chamber and be assented to, a bill with respect to national health and welfare, which takes care of the remainder of the pensions and health departs ment. There will be no Department of Pensions and National Health. My hon. friend will see that what is being done here is to make provision for the salaries of new Ministers of National Health and Welfare and of Veterans' Affairs. The moment the new departments are created the salary of the present Minister of Pensions and National Health will be dropped entirely from the salary list. In order in the meantime that the minister may be assured of his salary section 2 provides:
Until such date as the Department of National Health and Welfare Act and the Department of Veterans' Affairs Act, passed at the present session of parliament, come into force by proclamation of the governor in council, the salary of the Minister of Pensions and National Health shall be ten thousand dollars per annum.
In other words, he is continued on the list until the two new departments come into being. It simply comes down to making provision for the portfolio of reconstruction and one other additional portfolio.

It is a good thing the Prime Minister has the choice, because otherwise he might not fare very well.
I have no doubt the Prime Minister has considered a different arrangement in connection with the portfolio of Secretary of State for External Affairs. One must consider the heavy burdens a Prime Minister must bear, not only as first minister of the land, but also as President of the Privy Council. Added to that has been the work connected with the Department of External Affairs. Indications are that, as time goes on, that work will be more extended.
I am wondering if the Prime Minister would care to comment on the possibility of having a separate minister for the portfolio of Secretary of State for External Affairs? I do not raise the matter as one of immediate possibility, but I do so having in mind the fact that the Department of External Affairs will undoubtedly become more important as time goes by. I take it the Prime Minister has in mind, perhaps not for his government, but for succeeding administrations, the possibility of recommending a change in that regard.

I believe it was about a year ago I spoke about this matter, and indicated that, personally, I would greatly welcome having at an appropriate time the portfolio of external affairs held by another minister of the crown. But since the war began, it has been almost impossible to separate some of the questions which come before the government for consideration from the Prime Minister's office and the Department of External Affairs. It would have been very difficult for the Prime Minister from day to day to have done other than have most of his time taken up with matters relating to external affairs.
For this reason I have assumed the burden, one which I believe is heavier than anyone would wish to assume, unless he thought that in doing so he would serve some really helpful and useful purpose. Everything considered, I think it has been just as well not to have the change made at the present time. However, I do agree entirely with my hon. friend the leader of' the opposition that in a subsequent parliament whoever may have to do with these different positions would be wise if he were to seek a minister to fill the portfolio of external affairs, with duties apart altogether from those of the Prime Minister.

The President of the Council raises another matter. I believe this office was billed in the first instance by Sir John A. Macdonald, while he was Prime Minister, so that, in that way, he might have before him something in the nature of a survey of the work of the government as a whole. In the position of President of the Council, I have found that it has worked out in that way. I do not wish to delay the passage of this bill in committee, but I would make a few remarks with respect to new appointments to be made. In my years in public life, which go back some considerable time, I have always felt that in the choosing of cabinet ministers, prime ministers have too often paid more attention to geographical appointments than to making appointments with due regard to the callings of the men affected.
In this chamber, like the Prime Minister I am surrounded by lawyers, doctors and other professional men. To my left we see the party which is hoping to gain a few seats, if possible, and they are overwhelmed with schoolteachers and ministers of the gospel.

speechtext: Do not forget the farmers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SALARIES OF MINISTERS OF VETERANS' AFFAIRS AND RECONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
There are one or two. But they do not farm-except the people. I realize, of course, that anything we say would have very little effect on the Prime Minister's choice. But in the present cabinet-and I do not say this in any unkindly spirit-I do not see the representation I should like to see. In the dominion we find industry, agriculture and labour. These three groups compose the major part of our population. In my view the labour portfolio should be administered by one who knows labour, and agriculture by one who knows agriculture. The portfolio of national revenue is not, in my opinion, a legal portfolio at all. It has been my view that that is a portfolio suited to a business man, because the minister would deal with industry, with tariffs, with regulations connected with customs duties, and matters which are connected solely with the industrial life of the country.
The Minister of Public Works-and again I say this in the most kindly spirit-should be someone who is a builder, or who knows something about building. I do not think a lawyer is particularly well fitted to hold the portfolio of public works, simply because he has a legal mind. In the whole cabinet at the present time I do not find one man who has been engaged in industry. The nearest one would come to an industrialist is to be found in the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who was a contractor, builder and engineer.
It is my belief that the men who should administer departments in the post-war should be men who have not been particularly trained in law or medicine, but men who have been trained in the hard way in the departments over which they would have to preside. I believe the people would have more confidence in the new departments if men with practical knowledge of the various subjects involved were chosen to head those departments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SALARIES OF MINISTERS OF VETERANS' AFFAIRS AND RECONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
In the matter of the selection of ministers in a country as broad as Canada, and with interests as diverse in many parts, it is always necessary for a Prime Minister to have regard to questions of geography, race, religion and other considerations. The hon. member has introduced an additional consideration, namely that relating to callings or occupations. Within certain bounds it is true that considerations of the kind he has mentioned should weigh. But the weight to be given to them must necessarily largely depend upon the personnel of the house, and the number of persons of different occupations who are elected.
In choosing ministers of the crown I believe the best administration is to be achieved where regard is had first and foremost for the intelligence and integrity of the persons appointed. A man of ability, sound judgment and high attainments would to my mind fill much better any portfolio of government that might be allotted to him than could possibly be the case with others who might seem to have qualifications on the grounds of calling or occupation, but who did not have the required attainments in other ways.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
On several occasions I have referred to section 12, subsection 1, wherein the following words appear:
Subject to the approval of the minister, the board may issue to any person applying therefor a licence to operate a commercial air service.
I am not going to deal at any length to-day with the arguments heretofore advanced with regard to this section. Suffice it to say that the attitude which we on this side of the house have taken is that what should be a free and independent board set up for the purpose of determining rights in a quasi-judicial manner will in fact be a board entirely under the control of the minister, and we feel that to vest power in the minister such as will be vested under this section is arbitrary, dangerous and autocratic. I am not going into the arguments advanced in that behalf except to say this, that the board set up to grant licences as between various claimants will be a board apparently possessing powers but in fact having no powers except subject to the minister, with the result that any decision which this board would come to would be in effect the minister's own decision. The board, finding itself in the position of having three or four applicants for a licence, and determining that one certain applicant has the proper qualifications and is the most entitled to the licence, would make a decision thereon subject to the minister's approval; in effect the board would be a pawn in the minister's hand and a body which, while appearing to have powers, would be in effect .merely a stooge of the minister.
For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I wish to move:
That section 12, subsection 1, be amended by deleting the words in the first line thereof, namely "Subject to the approval of the minister",
-so as to set up a board which will have powers, a board which can make judicial or semi-judicial decisions without the control of the minister. An analogy would be to set up a court of law with power to make judgments but whose judgments would be effective only if the Minister of Justice agreed therewith; there would be in effect a denial of every principle on which out jurisprudence is founded.
This section is different from any section in corresponding legislation in either the United States or Great Britain. For that and other reasons which have been heretofore advanced I move the amendment in order to take away from the minister the right, in fact, to control decisions, judicial and semi-judicial, made by the board to the end that the board shall be free, impartial and uncontrolled.
