The amendment proposed and the government's policy represent two wholly opposite views of responsible government. The amendment proposes that the domain of air be taken out of the hands of government, taken away from parliament, and turned over to a board of three members appointed for a long term. This board, quite independent of the minister and of parliament, would then distribute the empire of air as would seem wise to the board. The view of the government is that responsibility for the domain of the air is a federal responsibility, having been so determined by the privy council of the United Kingdom, and that it shall be the responsibility of the government of the day. This board is intended to advise the government, to examine various applications and to determine points for or against each. The government will hardly act against the advice of the board. If it believes that the board has not chosen wisely, it may ask the board to reconsider. That is quite within the realm of possibility, and that has been the attitude with respect to appeals from the board of transport commissioners throughout the years. The privy council, while it has the right on appeal to reverse decisions, has never done so. It has never taken action on appeals from the board of transport commissioners except to refer a matter back for rehearing. My hon. friend says that this differs from legislation in the United States. That is not so. In the United States the authority considers applications from air lines and makes recommendations to the executive power. The executive power may accept such recommendations or refuse to accept them, but the power in the United States is in the executive, and not in the board. In the United Kingdom the matter of air line franchises is dealt with by a department of government just as had been the practice in Canada up to 1938. This is not an abrogation of power on the part of the minister. He has always had the power. He abrogated it to the board of transport commissioners, with certain restrictions, in 1938, but experience since that time has shown that it is desirable that the government should itself retain responsibility and exercise its judgment, in matters affecting air routes. As I say, we are presented with two totally different viewpoints, and if my

hon. friend presses his amendment the committee must choose which is preferable as a means of carrying on democratic government.

The difficulty is that the matter of developing air routes and assigning them involves questions of policy rather than questions of law. The board of transport commissioners have been simply judges interpreting a law. The board exercises no initiative in suggesting air routes, or in planning the development of the air system. That practice was a mistake. The fault was not in the board of transport commissioners; the fault was in the act which bound them too tightly to certain procedure. My hon. friend will observe that in this case we have not attempted to bind this board by elaborate procedure. Rather we have asked the board to develop its own procedure through experience, which I think is the only sound way to proceed.
Aeronautics Act

The purpose of this bill is to set up a board of three men who have a knowledge of air transport work, who have a knowledge of Canada, who have a knowledge of the problems which they will be expected to deal with. That board will be asked to advise the government on matters of policy, to study the maps of Canada and the maps of the world, to attend to every detail on air matters. I can assure my hon. friend that the pressure of problems 'arising in the air takes a very considerable part of any minister's time, and, with only the advice of the department officials available, I will say quite frankly it is not getting the attention at this moment that it deserves. As a result of this bill, we hope to bring in three men of sound judgment and solid background, of air transport knowledge, and we hqpe to make progress much more rapidly in the future than we have in the past. However, when this bill becomes law the government will continue to be responsible to parliament for any franchise in the air that may be awarded in the future.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Why was it necessary to give power to this new board to decide between applicants for a route? I can quite see that an advisory board might be of great assistance particularly since under section 15 of the Transport Act the governor in council had power to decide what routes should be flown. Why go farther and give this new board, which is not really a judicial board but an advisory board, the job of deciding between A and B as to who is to fly a particular route. Would it not be far better to leave that to the present board of transport commissioners, who would exercise their judgment in a judicial way, having in mind that there should not be undue competition and who was best qualified to fly a route and so on? It seems to me that would be a far wiser way to handle the matter.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
A decision of that kind is usually not a judicial one. There are a great many facts to be marshalled. The procedure in the United States is as follows. A certain route is opened for award. Applications are usually filed by every air line in the country. It takes many months, sometimes years, to sort out the applications. Each applicant must present a brief, which comes before the board. That brief gives reasons why the route should be awarded to the applicant's air line. We have been applicants at Washington ourselves; we know something of the procedure and something of the time element involved. The most careful study is made of the relative merits of each applicant, and in due course a finding with reasons is brought down as a

recommendation to the executive that the route be awarded to one of the applicants. I think the executive has always acted on the advice of the aeronautics authority, and I presume that the executive here will act on the advice of this board. The board has its own experts to advise it and has the time and the means to study the relative merits of each application, and is thus able to give the government a sound reason to support its recommendation. But to me the great important duty of the board is to study the development of air transport in Canada and to advise the government on a sound policy to be followed in that development, and to make sure that the development is pressed as rapidly as the equipment situation will permit.

speechtext:
May I touch on one matter in connection with the control of aeronautics by the dominion? The minister referred to the privy council decision, but the privy council did not make a decision on question No. 3, which was decided by the Supreme Court of Canada, and regarding which there was no decision made by the privy council; therefore the matter as to whether or not there is exclusive control in so far as regulation and control in the dominion parliament is concerned has not yet been decided by the privy council. Question No. 2 was as follows:
Is legislation of the parliament of Canada providing for the regulation and control of aeronautics generally within Canada, including flying operations carried on entirely within the limits of a province necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada, or of any province thereof, under the convention aforementioned, within the meaning of section 132 of the British North America Act, 1867?
That question was answered by the Supreme Court of Canada, but was not answered by the privy council; therefore the privy council judgment 1932 AC54, does . not decide the proposition that the minister has just stated. The answer of the majority of the Supreme Court of Canada was:
No if the word "generally" in the question was equivalent to "in every respect."
The minister by his own answer has advanced the strongest possible reason why this board should not be controlled by the minister. Under the Transport Act the board of transport commissioners are a semi-judicial body. The statement of the hon. member for Cape Breton South indicated that this body had acted in a way that was contrary to the law of this country; in fact, that it had acted improperly. The minister now says that suggestion is unfounded, but he does find fault with the board of transport commissioners.

Aeronautics Act
I would point out that the reason why he finds fault with them in so far as aviation is concerned is that their decisions were based on law and on the act and therefore were not satisfactory. What the minister tries to do by section 12, subsection 1, is to secure in his hands a board which inferentially will not be bound too tightly by the law or by the provisions of the act. In other words, he wants to have a board set up which ostensibly will be required to carry out the law in the act, but when it does, on occasion its decision may not be ratified by the minister in the decision arrived at. The minister may say that there is a similar principle in the United States. Let me say to him that there is no such principle in the Aeronautics Act of the United States; in the United States the executive and the legislative are separate; hence the provisions of that act.
The minister says that in Britain the department of government controls. Let the department of government control here. Why have a board to go through the motions? Why pay a board $10,000, $12,000, $14,000 a year for the purpose of going through motions, for the purpose ostensibly of carrying out the law but carried out only when the minister believes it should be carried out, while in other cases stretching the law or entirely disregarding it when the minister believes it is a matter oi policy to do so?
I object to the setting up of a board whose powers will be limited; who will not be permitted to comply with the law if the minister believes the law ought not to be complied with, and whose creation will permit the practice of discrimination in the awarding of valuable air franchises. The main function this board will perform, as far as the minister is concerned, is that it will recommend something that should be done. A board of three members, drawing large salaries, will be set up although we have a board now, the board of transport commissioners, who are far from overworked. They receive very considerable salaries, as they should in the position they occupy. We are to set up a new board, depriving it of the privilege of exercising judicial functions. We are going to take away from it the right to carry out sound principles of law, and of exercising sound discretion. We are going to set up a new board, whose members again will receive large salaries, for the purpose of making recommendations which cannot be carried into effect without the minister's approval. The minister speaks of ministerial responsibility, but that is not what we have here. This amounts to judicial irresponsibility,
if the board is set up in this form. There is nothing like this under any act of the parliament of Great Britain.
The minister says the administration of aviation concerns matters of policy, which is v the responsibility of the minister and the department. Then why set up the board, unless it be that we are creating a number of new positions at very fancy salaries, to be distributed at this time. I object to the setting up of the board in the first place as unnecessary; but if it is to be set up, then it should have power, responsibility, discretion and, as the hon. member for Carleton says, independence. Think of the possibilities of the position of this board. I am not in any way suggesting that the minister would have any ill-feeling against any group or applicant who might come before this board, but human nature being what it is, if a minister disliked any company or any individual he could arbitrarily refuse a licence, regardless of the qualifications of the company or the individual applying. If parliament grants the minister that power, in effect parliament thereby abdicates its right to the assurance that individuals appearing before a board set up by parliament shall not be denied justice.
The minister's only reply is that this novel change is introduced because we must look at the air situation throughout the world as well as in Canada, and matters of policy must be considered. Well, Mr. Chairman, policy is considered to-day. The governor in council sets up the routes, which means in effect that they are set up by the government of the day. They make the policy, as to where aviation facilities are to be provided, and the board decides as between various claimants for licences. I am going to ask the minister one very pointed question in regard to the -board of transport commissioners. He stated that the criticism of the hon. member for Cape Breton South was ill-founded. Does not the minister think the policy the government now seems bent upon pursuing will bring about in this country a rather chaotic condition in the days that lie ahead, with respect to transportation and communication? After all, there must be some integrating of the transportation facilities of a nation such as Canada.
The minister appears to be taking a retrograde step, if I may say so, because first of all he is separating the railways from air transportation and, in addition to that, he is taking away from the board of transport commissioners any powers connected with air routes. This involves at the same time a
fMr. Diefenbaker.]
further step in separating these two systems. I think the minister and government might very properly review and reconsider their position in this respect.
While I am not an expert in transportation matters, yet I believe even laymen who will look at the transportation problem in Canada cannot help seeing the difficulties, and I believe may justly express some fear of the future when there is no reasonable amount of integration among the various kinds of travel. If we are giving this new board certain powers and talcing away from the board of transport commissioners any jurisdiction it might have over air transportation, this board would have lesser powers, and would actually be just a good and obedient hired man for the minister. In plain, ordinary terms that is what the bill means. It will further emphasize the cleavage between two great modes of transportation.
The problem of general communications also comes to my mind, and I have in mind radio particularly. The suggestion has been made this year in the committtee or radio broadcasting that, in view of the fact that Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is in competition with privately owned stations, an independent board should be set up to adjudicate between the two. If in Canada we are to have a board of transport commissioners to handle matters connected with railway travel, and at the same time to have another board to handle air transportation, and another to handle communications, the government should watch carefully to see that this does not proceed too far. I would urge that the minister give this matter serious consideration before we embark upon setting up a variety of boards, the integration of which would become increasingly difficult in the years which lie ahead.
I raise my voice against the proposal of the minister as contained in section 12, and I shall support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre. This board must be one thing or another, as I see it. The minister is attempting to make it a part of several things, and when he gets finished with it it will end up, not as a board, but rather just another department under the minister.
There is no other way in which this can be interpreted. Certainly it is not the kind of board that the board of transport commissioners has set out to be. In effect this board is simply the chore boy of the minister. Air transportation, in its present condition, deserves something more by way of independence. It should have an independent board whereby everyone would be able to receive a fair deal. I am not suggesting that the

Aeronautics Act
minister would intentionally give anyone an unfair deal but, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre, human nature is human nature. I do not think it should be necessary for an applicant to have to approach any particular political party when he wishes to take action in this respect. He should be in a position to go to an independent body. That body would then give its decision, in the light of existing circumstances.
I would ask the minister to consider where all this is leading, from the point of view of a wide distribution of authority, and a wide distribution of the various measures controlling our transportation and communications. Mr. Chairman, I believe I should say a few words at this point. I am not conversant with civil air transportation, but I would look at that feature of the air transport board which establishes it as a judicial body deciding judicial questions.
Let us consider three different events. First, an applicant wants to get a licence. Instead of going to the air transport board directly he must go to the minister, to see that the application meets with the minister's
approval. The transport board must approve, too. If the applicant went to the board for instance, their decision would be governed by the minister's approval.
Those of us who believe in British institutions are proud of one thing, perhaps more than another, and that is the independence of our judicial bodies. Hon. members must keep in mind that a decision by the air transport board must meet with the approval of the minister of the day. When an applicant applies for something from the board he knows that the board must make a decision which will meet with the approval of the minister himself. How can an. applicant expect an impartial ruling from the board such as we would expect from our judiciary, under British institutions? How can an applicant expect to. get an opinion purely non-political and nonpartisan, and purely judicial, when that opinion is subject to the control of the minister?
Some talk about the control of parliament. Well, control of parliament is one thing, but control of the minister is another. There is a vast difference. I say that for the sake of efficiency a board must be independent. It must be assured that it cannot be accused of political influence, and it must not be subject to the approval of any one man or any one set of circumstances. Such a board should have the privileges extended to a judicial body. It should be their minds that speak; it should not be the mind of the minister that gives the verdict.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

I cannot understand why the government considers it necessary to adopt a totally different method of administering travel by air or air transportation from the one it has to administer travel by land and water. It is realized by all that when the end of the war comes there will be a considerable increase, a surge forward in transportation. A hundred years ago the United Kingdom went through such a surge forward in transportation by land. Sir Robert Peel or whoever was prime minister in those days did not see fit to put the administration of transportation into the hands of one of his ministers. Schemes were considered on their merits before a parliamentary committee.
We carried on somewhat in the same way in this country. Where a railway extension is contemplated a bill comes before this house and is sent to the railway committee. I do

Aeronautics Act

not understand why it is necessary to have a totally different form of government for schemes by air as compared with government for schemes in connection with other forms of transportation. Why is it necessary for so much power to be put into the hands of a minister; it does not matter who the minister may be? subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, speaking to the amendment I would remind my hon. friend, as he has already reminded the committee, of the method of granting franchises for surface transportation. A bill is prepared, brought to parliament, sent to a committee which in turn reports to parliament, and then parliament decides whether the franchise shall or shall not be granted. The purpose of this amendment would be to take that power, exercised by parliament in the case of railways, and in the case of our airways turn it over to a bureaucracy not responsible to parliament. It has been said that the members of the board can be dismissed for cause, but I wonder what the public reaction would be if the board were dismissed because it departed from the wishes of parliament in the placing of franchises. I hardly think that that would be considered as good cause for the dismissal of high placed public servants, under the practices of a British parliament.
Perhaps I can explain why bills for air lines are not brought to parliament. The practice is not new, dating back to 1918 or 1919. Air is a much more fluid means of transportation than transportation by land. A railway franchise is a permanent thing. Rails are laid down, and the operator is bound to operate trains over them until relieved of his responsibility by the board of transport commissioners, or by some other authorized body. An air line operates into an area. In the case of mining developments, a service may be required one year and not be required the next year. It would hardly be practical to require that bills be presented to parliament to establish air lines, particularly into remote areas.
Since 1918, when the Aeronautics Act was passed, it has been the function of the minister responsible for the administration of that act to allocate franchises. As a matter of practice the minister has functioned by obtaining orders in council. That practice was changed in 1938 by a bill which was presented under my sponsorship, and that authority was placed in the hands of the board of transport commissioners.
The difficulty is that the board of transport commissioners are in essence a judicial body. They have no staff to help them to form
[Mr. Stirling.J
policies. They were attempting to deal with airway problems in a purely legalistic way.* The proof of the pudding is in the eating, and the proof of the pudding has not been in the interests of the development of our airways, at least in my humble opinion. This bill is an attempt to set up a strong advisory body t-o deal with policy matters, and also to act as a semi-judicial body for the final determination of matters that are judicial in character. We are adopting a form that has worked well in the country to the south of us, which country has seen the greatest development of airways of any country in the world.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: It is not in effect there.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

It is in effect there, if my hon. friend will not interrupt. We are following a pattern which has worked well on this continent. My hon. friend states that in the United Kingdom there is no board, that these matters are dealt with departmentally. I would remind him that the United Kingdom is a small area and that internal civil aviation there is not a problem of great magnitude. Canada is a country of tremendous distances, and it is thinly settled. After having struggled with this problem for some eight or nine years, I can assure my hon. friend that our problem is a huge one. Any minister administering the Aeronautics Act to-day needs expert advice; he needs the help of men who are able to concentrate on one problem, the development of airways.
The purpose of this bill is to set up that sort of support for the minister who will be responsible for the Aeronautics Act. I am satisfied that this is a constructive measure.
I believe it to be a measure that will make for the development of our airways, a measure that will make for a sound air policy to guide that development. Therefore, I must oppose the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lake Centre. If his amendment were adopted, I believe there would be no course open to the government but to abandon the bill now before the committee.

The difficulty is that we are creating something that is neither fish nor fowl. This board can have neither an independent viewpoint nor independent judicial powers. As I say, we are simply building up an organization that is neither fish nor fowl, an organization which will have no function that it can exercise in the independent way we would like to see it exercised as far as judicial decisions are concerned.

I mentioned that the experience in the United States had been similar to the experience in Canada. The need for divorcing the two has arisen out of our experience in Canada. The decision to be made therefore is, as I have said before, whether we shall have a monopoly of the air ways in the hands of the railways. The railways are naturally interested in developing transportation by rail. The question is, with complete monopolistic control of the air, would they be equally interested in developing our airways? Another question is whether we should turn over the empire of the air to those who control the empire of surface transportation? We must recall that pioneering of the airways has been performed by small operators. The railways never have been pioneers of the air. The small operator, serving a territory with area within his capacity to serve, has proved to be a very satisfactory means of developing air transportation. In my opinion, this small operator should have a chance in the air, and steps should be taken to see that our airways do not drift into monopolistic control; that is a matter of convenience to the public rather than benefit to any interest.
I believe that the public is better served by the small operator whose well-being depends on giving good service to his area. That is the purpose behind the bill; it is a purpose that

I wish to continue this same line of argument, Mr. Chairman, and it will not take more than a minute or two. The minister has said that he does not want to give a monopoly to the railways. I am in complete accord with him on that because, as I tried to point out when I spoke on this bill before, it has been the old bush pilots, the small operator, the fellow who had two or three aircraft who built up Canadian aviation. The big transcontinental operators come later. Because we do not want to give the railways ,-a monopoly, is it necessary to divorce the railways from the long haul aircraft business? Surely traffic whether by air, sea or rail will flow to the most efficient and cheapest method. It seems to me that in the long haul transportation, the transcontinental field, the railways are singularly equipped to dove-tail their [DOT]operations in with the operations in the air; whereas the company that does nothing but -fly aircraft into the north country, where there is no other method of transportation, does not and cannot fear competition by the major companies, because the small company can always beat the big company due to its flexibility.
I think this bill is based on the wrong premise. The small company with a few aircraft and low overhead can give service to an outlying mine or an outlying community, or they can start a service to a new mining area or a new agricultural area. Once that is established and heavy traffic moves in, it becomes the duty of the railways to go in and haul that heavy traffic. But at the present time, because of the peculiarity of our great as yet untapped resources, the bill says that we will divorce the railway companies from all air transportation. I say that there is room for both of those operators, room for the railway operators operating on the main trunk lines, and I think they can be dove-tailed quite efficiently into railway operations; but the small feeder lines that perhaps have no accurate schedule-and remember we gained first place in the world in air freight by these small companies-will not be injured by the railways. The railways will never be able to compete with these small companies because the small companies will provide a flexibility of service with which the railways could never compete. They will be able to take you in whether you arrive at eleven o'clock or at any time, whether you want to take in a boiler or a piece of machinery. They will take you in and let you off anywhere. They are like a taxi service;

they will take you anywhere you want to go. No railway company is going to be interested in that type of service; but that small company is not going to be interested in and could never be interested in the major transcontinental or heavy traffic air arteries. I know they have done it in the United States and have made a success of it. Because they have done it is no reason why we should do it. The minister has not explained why it is good policy for us to follow completely the United States practice. The bush pilot, the small individual operator, is, I grant, the main operator. speechtext: I want to offer the minister my full support in this proposal to set up an aeronautics board to control civil aviation and grant licences for any additional interurban or intermunicipal air lines. There is a distinct similarity between the provisions of this measure and those in effect in Ontario, and perhaps other provinces as well, in regard to the granting of franchises for the operation of bus lines. I think back to 1921 and 1922 in the province of Ontario when we had very little control over bus and truck transport, and not as much control over the registration and regulation of private automobiles as we have to-day. I sat on a committee of the Ontario legislature. We spent many months drawing up an entirely new highway traffic act which has been changed very little since that time. We then set up regulations for buses, for private traffic lines, and prepared to give franchises to the bus lines operating on various highways in Ontario. Toward the conclusion of our meetings I suggested that perhaps it might be well if we asked the railways to come in and give us the benefit of any surveys that they might have made of bus and truck traffic. We did approach the railways and they said they had nothing to submit. So far as passengers were concerned the bus traffic was not a particular menace to them at that time, but we see what has happened since. When the buses really became a heavy carrying traffic organization in the province the railways came into the picture and asked for franchises to operate either in competition with existing lines or exclusive lines on certain highways in the province. Those have been granted, and we find that to-day we have built up in Ontario one of the finest systems of bus, truck and railway transportation of any province of the Dominion of Canada. They are doing it in competition with each other; they are doing it in such a way that those who travel by or ship by any one of those means of transportation are getting the very highest type of service. Would the minister indicate why provision should be made at all for an appeal from a board of three to a single individual? Why not leave it with the board and let its decision be final? The hon. member for York-Sunbury drew an analogy which to my mind was compelling, in connection with the operation of the Income War Tax Act. The only justification I have been given for that course of conduct-and' I raised this question before I was ever a member of this house-was explained to me in this way. Subsection 10 is even more objectionable than subsection 8. This provides for an appeal where a licence has been suspended. Subsection 8 referred to the issuing of a licence. If an applicant did not receive his licence, he might appeal; but subsection 10 covers the man who has actually received his licence, and has then had it cancelled or suspended. Again the appeal is only to the minister. There is a further power of cancellation or suspension in section 13 of the act, a power which is even more drastic than the one we are discussing. The board is authorized under section 13 to investigate all existing licences, and is given carte blanche to suspend or cancel any of those licences. I presume, if there is any appeal at all in the event of such drastic action, it must be to the minister.
I suggest to the committee that this is a clear case where the appeal should be to the governor in council, and not to the minister. In the legislation being brought before the house there is a distinct trend away from cabinet responsibility, and toward giving ministers absolute out-and-out power in everything. I suggest that is a dangerous trend, and one which should be stopped. I presume this practice has arisen because during the war years the government has passed so many orders in council it has simply got into the habit of doing things by short-cuts.
However, the bill before the committee is not a measure for the war period. This is a

measure concerning civil aviation, and it sets out the domestic aviation policy of Canada for the post-iwar years. We should not have any short-cut war measures in connection with this bill. What it amounts to is this, that anybody wishing to obtain a licence or anybody who, having obtained a licence, has had it cancelled or suspended, will have to go hat-inhand to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, or whoever is in charge of civil aviation at that time, and try to make a good fellow of himself, in the hope that he may get some consideration. That is not a good enough way to build up a great system of civil aviation in Canada. It cannot be done in that way.
I move in amendment, therefore:
That subsection 10 of section 12 of Bill No. 133 be amended by substituting for the word "minister" therein the words "governor in council".

As I said before, the purpose is to set up a board that will control civil aviation. We will assume that the government intends to place in charge of civil aviation in this country a board that will carefully consider its position and make its judgments after due examination. This bill gives the appellant the right to go to the minister and tell its story. It can go to the minister as a matter of right. If the minister believes that the board has acted too harshly, he can ask the board to reconsider the matter. This is a similar procedure to that explained 'by the Minister of National Revenue. He can ask the board to have another look at the problem. I think that is as far as any minister would logically go. From my own experience in government, I do not believe that any minister, on his own authority, would reverse the finding of a board.
I think what he would do is just what the governor in council has been doing for years with appeals from the board of transport commissioners. The minister would ask the board to reexamine its finding. The reason why the minister is mentioned in the bill, rather than the governor in council, is to have appeals dealt with expeditiously. Appeals to the governor in council become automatic, because the delay involved works on the side of the applicant. This delay has prevented the removal of rail lines which should have been removed; it has prevented the abandonment of services which deserved to be abandoned. It has simply been another way of getting an extension of several months. An appeal to the minister can be made quickly, and it cannot be made the means of delay, as is the case with railway applications.

speechtext: Section 13 is drastic and I think the minister should, explain why it is included in the bill. This section gives the air transport board the power to cancel or suspend any licence in existence at the time the board commences its work. In 1938 when the Transport Act was passed setting up the board of transport commissioners just the reverse procedure was followed. Those companies that had licences continued to operate, but now for some reason or another all licences have to be reviewed and the board may cancel or suspend any of them. Why is it necessary to take such drastic powers? Are there licences outstanding which the minister thinks should be cancelled?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The purpose of this section is to allow the board a reasonably free hand to reorganize the air transport services of Canada. I can assure my hon. friend that the section in question will not be used in an arbitrary way, but the board must have power to regroup the air lines in a more orderly way than the present.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Is there any appeal from these cancellations?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No appeal.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I understand that the licences are from year to year in any event.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Not necessarily; they are for such time as the minister may decide.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Are not licences granted
yearly?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes, that is true; they are renewed every year.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Why the necessity of this section? It could not be longer than a year before all licences would expire automatically. When the licences are renewed the conditions which the minister wishes to impose could be put in the new licences. Why give the board the power to cancel existing licences?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: This is just to serve notice that the board have the power. A licence could be allowed to expire and not be renewed, but it has never been the practice to do that. Notice is being served that the board has the right to cancel licences.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Could not that be done by letters to the licencees? There are not a great number of them. It seems to me that that would be a far better way to do it rather than putting an arbitrary section of this type in the statute. This section will be of no value once the board has reviewed all the licences. I suggest that it would be far better to send out a letter pointing out that all licences will expire at the end of the year and that they will not be renewed without further consideration being given to them.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The government believes it desirable to serve notice on all air lines that the new board will have the power to cancel franchises. It seems a desirable way. Simply a letter from an official of the department to the licencees might not be considered sufficient notice.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: They all know now that their licence is good only for a year, do they not?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: It is a public announcement that the crown is going in for government control.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
If the government is
allowed to regroup the present lines under this section, what provision is there for compensation in case any particular line is damaged?

There is no compensation for a franchise. Franchises are not for sale. They are the property of the crown. There is no compensation for the cancelling of a franchise. Compensation may arise out of facilities in-
Aeronautics Act

stalled on air lines or equipment used in the operation of air lines, but franchises are not for sale.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Where is the compensation, then, in case the facilities are no longer usable by that company or nothing can be got for them in case they are sold?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
That will have to be
considered.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
If the minister expects
that civil aviation in this country is going to develop and there are going to be any number of private lines, whether they be large or small, I certainly believe that the provisions of this bill as we now have them before us will prevent any capital from ever flowing into the civil aviation or transport industry in Canada. It will remain a pure government monopoly, and it will probably wither, as nearly all government monopolies do, because they have not the enterprise, vigour and freedom that private enterprise gives. One of the first things that is going to happen from the passing of this measure is that young men, the ones with vision in this industry, will leave Canada, resign from the existing private air transport companies, and go to the south. Already many of them have had offers from the companies there; and we are going to find that the air transport industry here will be on a much diminished scale compared with what it would be if we allowed free enterprise and permitted these various companies some assurance that the investments which will be made in them will be given a fair opportunity to earn a return. As it is, the minister says that they have a licence for only one year, which may be cancelled at any time; yet as sensible people they believe that the government or this department will adopt a sensible attitude, and that the privilege or the licence will be renewed from year to year. Now the minister wishes to insert in this bill clauses which will allow their facilities to be taken over without any compensation whatsoever. All I can say is that this bill is a complete warning to private capital to stay entirely out of the air transport industry in Canada.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: In section 12, subsection 2, the minister has provided that no company engaged in any other form of transportation shall have an air line, and when he made his speech in March in which he gave the policy of the government on domestic aviation he said that the railway companies were to be forced out of the air business within a year after the war. This section 14 goes much further than that; not only does it purport to cancel licences which have been issued to railway companies, but it cancels all licences.. Why is it necessary to do that?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I have great confidence that the board would not issue a licence and then cancel it, except for cause.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
As I explained earlier in the debate, the practice in the past has been to-

Aeronautics Act
assist the establishment of a new line by granting a subsidy through the post office-a subsidy, rather than a payment for services rendered. The post office objects to the principle-I think the principle is not very sound- of paying too high a price for the transportation of mail simply for the purpose of assisting the establishment of a new air line. The policy which the government intends to follow in future is that the post office will pay a reasonable amount for the carriage of mail. If a further subsidy is required, to permit the establishment of the line, the subsidy will be paid as a subsidy from funds voted by parliament for that purpose. We believe that is a much more honest way of subsidizing new operations, than to do so by giving an abnormally large rate for the carriage of mail.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Does this change in principle mean that the T.C.A. contract with the post office will now be revised according to the new principle?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Will my hon. friend sit down, please? We like wisdom, but not too much of it at one time. My hon. friend knows very well that the post office does not subsidize the T.C.A. In the initial stages, it did subsidize T.C.A. to the extent that it paid more for the carriage of' air mail than it received as revenue from air mail; but that situation has vastly changed, and to-day T.C.A. is a source of revenue to the post office rather than the subject of subsidy.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I am merely asking the minister whether or not this new principle which he thinks is fairer-the post office having objected to the principle of it being represented as subsidizing the T.C.A., even though it may work in reverse at times-will apply to a renegotiated contract between T.C.A. and the post office.

speechtext:
In so far as men returning from overseas are concerned, handicapped as they will be by lack of capital,
is it intended under this section that capital assistance shall be given them to enable them to commence or develop or carry on civil aviation? Recently, in an interview or a statement by the minister, published in Canadian Aviation, he referred to the matter of capital assistance. I rise now to ask whether it is intended to be the policy of the department or of the minister that capital assistance shall be given these men; for if that is not the policy I cannot see how these men returning from overseas, with merely a few hundred or a thousand dollars at the outset, will be able to commence a development of the kind suggested by the roseate picture which the minister drew when he originally outlined the policy with regard to aviation.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I have more confidence than my hon. friend in the men returning from overseas.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I do not know so much about that.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The men returning from overseas after the last war established air lines and did very well for a considerable number of ye^rs. I am not altogether sure that the men returning from this war will not have as much initiative as those men. However, this section will give the board the authority to recommend to the government that assistance be given to newly established air lines, whether capital or by way of operating subsidy. The power is there to draw on funds appropriated by parliament for either purpose, but I do not suggest that any group of airmen can expect as a matter of right to have the government furnish all the capital that will be needed for the operation. That is not the intention. The purpose of a small operation is to make sure that investment in the enterprise will be an inducement to the operator to give service to the area for which he is responsible. That financial inducement is a desirable part of any small private enterprise that will have a part in the plan for the future.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the minister to make available to the men who return from overseas aircraft that might be used for civil aviation, selling those aircraft on a time basis so as to enable them to finance themselves in the initial stages? When the war is over, large numbers of aircraft owned by the Canadian people will be available for civil aviation purposes, and I suggest that consideration be given to permitting the sale of them on a time basis
Aeronautics Act'

to these men to enable them to have at least certain facilities available so that they can establish for themselves air services, whether on a small or on a large basis.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: It is the policy of the government to-day to sell used military aircraft. It is doing so every day, and arrangements can be made for sale on time, but it would be very unwise for any group of returned men to buy used military aircraft to start a civil line. Military aircraft are not suitable for the purpose, and therefore I would not care to say anything to-night that would suggest to returned men that the way to establish a civil airline is by the use of military equipment. Returning men will be much wiser to buy proper aircraft, built for the purpose, and I have no doubt that the government will find ways and means of giving such assistance as may be needed to enable them to do so.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
In the wording of th'e section there is nothing to prevent the governor in council from authorizing the minister to grant a subsidy to T.C.A. The reason why I bring this question up is this. In the Winnipeg Free Press of April 11 there appears the following:
An extraordinary feature of aviation is the proportion of the total costs borne by the taxpayer on the one hand and the operating companies on the other. Startling examples of this have been given in the Free Press. For instance, the capital of Trans-Canada Air Lines is about $4^ millions, compared with the $96 millions carried by the public in the shape of airports, emergency landing fields, weather services, beacons and the like.
So that T.C.A. shows a small nominal profit on a very nominal capital of four and a half millions, and yet it has a service of $96 million provided for it of a capital nature. One would say, before this bill was introduced, that these services would be available to other air transport companies, but according to the terms of this bill we find that other companies will be divested of their air transport facilities and that any new capital that might enter the field will be frightened away. I would ask the minister the question, coupling with it the question I have already put to him, whether he will be allowed to bonus T.C.A. under this section.
I do not often use T.C.A., but at Easter I was at the airport at Lethbridge coming back from Calgary and there I saw a T.C.A. plane being serviced by an American army truck with gasoline. I could not help wondering what an American army truck, no doubt at the cost of the United States, was doing servicing our T.CA. planes. Perhaps there was an arrangement, but it seemed most extraordinary. When we got to North Bay, where we had to get

off, I saw, as a small item of expense, a safe in the ofiice marked "Canadian National Railways". One wonders who pays for what in T.C.A., and whether the profit is a real profit or actually comes from other public sources such as the publicly-owned Canadian National Railways. I would ask the minister how it is that these items can be reconciled with fair management and with a fair table of operating costs which are directly applicable to T.C.A. and not in the shape of indirect bonuses at the present time.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: So far as I know, T.C.A. is not bonused by the United States government. Lethbridge is on the northwest staging route, and if my hon. friend will follow that route he will find American trucks servicing Canadian planes and Canadian trucks servicing American planes, but more Canadian trucks servicing American planes than vice versa. I hope that explains why, on the northwest staging route, which handles some eighty per cent American planes to twenty per cent Canadian planes, the situation referred to can take place. As regards the safe in the T.C.A. office, I suppose it is a matter of saving money by buying a second-hand safe or perhaps borrowing a safe. At any rate, that is not a large transaction. My hon. friend sits in the committee that examines T.C.A. affairs each year, and since he is acquainted with the operations of the line I do not need to explain them to him.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: Because of the fact that ships are able to pick 'up freight in central Ontario, take it down the St. Lawrence and around to Vancouver, we have a cheaper shipping rate to Vancouver by water than to Alberta by rail. In Some cases it is cheaper to ship to Vancouver by water and then to Alberta by rail than to send a shipment direct by rail to Alberta. What is the reason for that?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: The rates charged by rail and water transportation companies have been subject to the control of the board of transport commissioners since the Transport Act was enacted in 1938. That was one of the main objects in mind in passing that act. There are differentials of all kinds in the rates for the transportation of goods by rail; there are differentials in the rates for transportation by water, and there are differentials as between rail and water transportation. These rates are established by the board of transport commissioners, who have the advice of the rate experts of different transportation companies, who consult with the experts of the board. I have not before me the details or the schedules of all these rates, but they are made by order of the board and are subject to appeal if anyone is dissatisfied with them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Are all the ports
of Canada under the jurisdiction of the dominion government?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
All ports are subject to
some control under some laws of the dominion, but I think the hon. gentleman means to ask whether all ports are under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board. The answer is that not all ports are under their jurisdiction.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: Aeroplanes are out of the picture now, as far as this board is concerned?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: Then who is to be responsible for the regulation of air traffic in the various ports? I am thinking of the Toronto harbour, which is under the control of the Toronto harbour commission. Who is to be responsible for the regulation of air traffic in that harbour?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: The aeronautics board.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Might I ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply who is to have jurisdiction over the coming and going of aeroplanes in a harbour such as that of Toronto?

Quebec Election

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: The city of Toronto owns and administers the airport under the regulations of the air transport board. All aviation is carried on under the direction of federal authority.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: : I have in mind particularly the operation of seaplanes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: They come under the control of the air transport board.	-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
WTho will have the final say as to how they are to come and go?
Mr. HOW^E: The air transport board.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: The harbour commissioners will have nothing whatever to do with it?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
The harbour commissioners will operate the seaplane base, just as they operate the land plane base, as the owners; they will direct traffic in connection with both, in accordance with the rules laid down by the air transport board.
IMr. ROSS (St. Paul's): They will direct traffic of the air boats, not the steam boats.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: The harbour of Toronto, so far as navigation by water is concerned, is independent in making its regulations for incoming and outgoing boats. I understood my hon. friend to ask whether rates for transportation of goods into that 'harbour would be under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners. I believe they will continue under the jurisdiction of that board, inasmuch as it has 'been given jurisdiction by the Transport Act of 1938. This change will not affect the movement of goods into or out of the port of Toronto by water.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: As I understand it, the 'harbour commissioners have the regulation of all traffic in the harbour.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: We shall now have two controls in Toronto harbour. The board connected with civil aviation will now come into the picture and, I suppose, will make regulations. I understand that the harbour commissioners will have to carry those out. Is that correct? Who will have the final say in the matter?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
I thought the minister was going to answer.
Mr. ROS'S (St: Paul's): I thought so, too. I should like to know something about it, as to how it is to be arranged.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES FROM JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: May I explain the air matter. The owner of an airport who is also the operator of the airport, has charge of traffic on that airport. But there are certain rules of the air laid down by the air transport board, and those rules must be obeyed. They are made in the interests of safety, and the operator of an airport must carry them out. If an airport is licensed, to maintain that licence it must live up to the traffic and safety rules laid dlown by the air transport board. Similarly, railroads must operate according to safety regulations laid down by the board of transport commissioners, and marine traffic must be regulated in the interest of safety, according to the rules laid down by the Department of Transport at Ottawa.
